But it speaks to parents’ long-standing fears about vaccines, even though the idea that giving vaccines one at a time is safer lacks a strong scientific basis. The CDC recommends children get one dose of MMR at 12-15 months of age and a second dose at age 4-6 years. Seeing the value of fewer injections, the trivalent MMR vaccine has been given in combination since 1971 and became the only option around 2008. The MMR has a long safety record, with some evidence the combination may even yield a stronger immune response. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the uncertainty among Colorado parents regarding vaccine safety and necessity, particularly the MMR vaccine. analysis.methods: The methods include qualitative data collection through interviews and observations, with no specific laboratory or statistical procedures mentioned.
analysis.main_results: The main results show that parents in Colorado value vaccine customization, with some opting for fewer injections or specific vaccines based on perceived risks. analysis.summary_en: This study explores parental concerns about vaccine safety and customization in Colorado, highlighting the challenges of recent executive orders on vaccine access. Qualitative research shows that parents value vaccine choice and customization, with some opting for fewer injections or specific vaccines based on perceived risks. The findings suggest that policies should consider the practical and logistical challenges faced by parents and healthcare providers.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究探讨了科罗拉多州家长对麻疹、腮腺炎和风疹联合疫苗安全性和必要性的不确定性,特别是针对MMR疫苗。背景强调了家长对疫苗接种个性化的需求,以及最近的行政命令可能对疫苗接种可及性和选择权产生的潜在影响。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究采用定性研究方法,包括对科罗拉多州家长、儿科医生、研究人员和政策制定者的访谈,以及对疫苗接种诊所和家长及医疗提供者的教育活动的观察。
elements_zh.methods: 研究方法包括通过访谈和观察进行的定性数据收集,未提及具体的实验室或统计程序。
elements_zh.main_results: 主要结果表明,科罗拉多州的家长重视疫苗接种的个性化,有些家长选择减少接种次数或根据所感知的风险选择特定疫苗。研究还报告称,自疫情以来,科罗拉多州的疫苗接种豁免率有所上升,其疫苗接种率低于全国平均水平。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将研究结果解释为表明家长对疫苗安全性和个性化接种的担忧是重要的,而最近的行政命令可能会无意中使疫苗接种变得更加复杂。研究的新颖之处在于对家长决策过程的详细洞察以及他们所面临的挑战。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果提醒人们注意可能限制疫苗接种可及性的政策,强调了提供清晰且一致的公共卫生信息的必要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其定性性质,以及所采访家长样本可能存在选择偏差。由于缺乏定量数据且主要关注家长的观点,证据强度中等。

papers.full_text: It takes a lot to knock football out of the headlines in Pittsburgh. But reports of measles cases, exposure alerts and calls for residents to double-check their vaccination status have dominated local news since August 2026. My office at Allegheny College, where I am an epidemiologist, is within a few steps of a classroom dedicated to Dr. Thomas Francis. Francis coordinated the entire polio vaccine field trial, which included 1.8 million children, and deemed the polio vaccine “safe, effective, potent.” As of Sept. 14, 2026, the Pennsylvania Department of Health has confirmed 693 measles cases across 38 of the state’s 67 counties this year, including 133 hospitalizations and four deaths among unvaccinated residents. That compares with 16 cases statewide in all of 2025. Allegheny County reported its first case tied to the current outbreak in August, when the county health department warned of a potential exposure at UPMC Children’s Hospital’s emergency department. Two confirmed cases were diagnosed on Aug. 27, 2026, but the patients left the county afterward. Pittsburgh is where Dr. Jonas Salk developed the first polio vaccine on the campus of the University of Pittsburgh. Children throughout the Pittsburgh area, including my father, lined up to participate in the Salk vaccine trials in 1954. That history offers a useful lens for understanding today’s measles outbreak: what’s driving it, how it spreads, and what residents in the Pittsburgh area need to know. Measles, explained Measles is one of the oldest and most contagious diseases. In fact, measles was around when the Egyptian pyramids were being built. Archaeological evidence shows the measles virus in the Tigris and Euphrates river valley in 3000 B.C.E. Measles is an acute respiratory virus. If an unvaccinated individual who has never had measles is exposed to the measles virus, they will likely become sick. Measles easily spreads through the air. Infected individuals are contagious 3-5 days before symptoms occur, a transmission mechanism known as asymptomatic spread. Viral particles remain active and infectious for up to two hours after a person with measles leaves a room. Symptoms of measles include a fever as high as 105 degrees Fahrenheit, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots, which are small white or bluish-white spots that appear on the inside of the cheeks before the measles rash breaks out on the skin. These spots are the defining diagnostic feature of measles. Measles also results in a rash, known as a “bucket of paint rash” because it looks like someone spilled a bucket of red paint over the head of the sick person. The rash is not contagious. This disease spreads when someone breathes in the virus. Before there was a vaccine for measles, upward of 3 million people – mostly children – were infected in the U.S. each year, 48,000 were hospitalized, and as many as 500 died. Measles was eliminated in the United States through vaccination in 2000, meaning person-to-person spread of the disease was disrupted. However, due to declining vaccination rates, measles is once again spreading throughout Pennsylvania, resulting in approximately four times as many measles cases in 2026 within the state as in the previous 30 years combined. Measles vaccination rates need to be above 95% to prevent the disease from spreading. The current outbreak has affected a majority of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties, an indicator that even small declines in vaccination coverage result in large outbreaks. The MMR vaccine is covered at no cost by most private insurance plans and is available free of charge to Medicaid-insured, uninsured or underinsured children at any of Pennsylvania’s 59 state health centers. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends children receive two doses by ages 4 to 6 to ensure protection against measles. Allegheny County’s kindergarten MMR vaccination rate was 91.8% for the 2025-26 school year – below the 95% threshold needed to stop measles from spreading and part of a decline the county health department has tracked for more than a decade. If you’re exposed to measles If you are vaccinated or have had measles, there is little risk – about 3% – that you will develop measles if exposed to the virus. There is no need to quarantine, but even vaccinated people should watch for symptoms of disease. For people who are unvaccinated, including infants, the risk of developing a measles infection after exposure is approximately 90%. Unvaccinated individuals need to quarantine. Local health departments require them to stay away from others for 21 days to prevent the asymptomatic spread of disease. If an individual in quarantine becomes ill, they will begin a minimum 14-day isolation. Measles is a serious disease. Approximately 20% of people who get it will develop pneumonia; many will require hospitalization, and a few will die. Each measles case costs our healthcare system approximately US$43,000, according to a Johns Hopkins systematic review of outbreaks in 18 states. The measles virus also has the ability to suppress one’s immune system. This means that after a bout of measles, survivors can be left more vulnerable to other infections they were previously protected against, sometimes for months or even years afterward. In order to prevent measles from spreading in our communities, at least 95% of the population must be vaccinated. The MMR vaccine was designed to prevent an individual from developing measles. But there is an added bonus: When the majority of a population is vaccinated, there are community-wide effects, mainly that community transmission of measles will begin to decline. Pittsburgh helped end one vaccine-preventable epidemic 70 years ago. The current measles outbreak could be a test of whether the local history still means something for vaccination rates today.

papers.title: Clinical Spectrum and Electroencephalographic Correlation in Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis: A Case Series
papers.abstract: Background: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) is a fatal, progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent, aberrant measles virus infection in the central nervous system. Characterized by cognitive deterioration, behavioral abnormalities, progressive motor deficit, and stereotyped slow myoclonic jerks, its clinical hallmarks are intricately linked to classic electroencephalographic (EEG) periodic slow-wave complexes (Radermecker complexes). Case Presentation: We report a series of four distinct clinical presentations of SSPE Case 1 describes a 20-year-old male with initial focal myoclonic seizures, asymmetric hemiparesis, cognitive decline, subsequent progression to generalized myoclonus, and typical generalized Radermecker complexes post-intrathecal interferon-alpha therapy. Case 2 illustrates an unimmunized 10-year-old boy presenting with classic scholastic failure, prominent axial and proximal appendicular slow myoclonus, gait impairment, and stereotypic high-voltage periodic slow complexes. Case 3 details an 18-year-old female with a confounding history of hydrocephalus requiring surgical decompression, presenting with scholastic decline, periodic slow-wave discharges, and slow myoclonus. Case 4 outlines an atypical, protracted decade-long course in a 20-year-old male misdiagnosed with primary psychiatric illness and movement disorders before presenting with severe cognitive failure, gait cessation, and classic periodic discharges. Discussion & Conclusion: These cases demonstrate the broad phenotypic spectrum of SSPE-spanning classic juvenile presentation, focal onset, neurosurgical confounders, and protracted psychiatric-extrapyramidal masquerades. Electroencephalography remains the pivotal real-time neurophysiological biomarker. Early clinico-electrophysiological suspicion is mandatory to avoid catastrophic diagnostic delays.
papers.journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

papers.title_zh: 亚急性硬化性全脑炎的临床表现谱及其与脑电图的相关性:病例系列
papers.source_body_en: Background: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) is a fatal, progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent, aberrant measles virus infection in the central nervous system. Characterized by cognitive deterioration, behavioral abnormalities, progressive motor deficit, and stereotyped slow myoclonic jerks, its clinical hallmarks are intricately linked to classic electroencephalographic (EEG) periodic slow-wave complexes (Radermecker complexes). Case Presentation: We report a series of four distinct clinical presentations of SSPE Case 1 describes a 20-year-old male with initial focal myoclonic seizures, asymmetric hemiparesis, cognitive decline, subsequent progression to generalized myoclonus, and typical generalized Radermecker complexes post-intrathecal interferon-alpha therapy. Case 2 illustrates an unimmunized 10-year-old boy presenting with classic scholastic failure, prominent axial and proximal appendicular slow myoclonus, gait impairment, and stereotypic high-voltage periodic slow complexes. Case 3 details an 18-year-old female with a confounding history of hydrocephalus requiring surgical decompression, presenting with scholastic decline, periodic slow-wave discharges, and slow myoclonus. Case 4 outlines an atypical, protracted decade-long course in a 20-year-old male misdiagnosed with primary psychiatric illness and movement disorders before presenting with severe cognitive failure, gait cessation, and classic periodic discharges. Discussion & Conclusion: These cases demonstrate the broad phenotypic spectrum of SSPE-spanning classic juvenile presentation, focal onset, neurosurgical confounders, and protracted psychiatric-extrapyramidal masquerades. Electroencephalography remains the pivotal real-time neurophysiological biomarker. Early clinico-electrophysiological suspicion is mandatory to avoid catastrophic diagnostic delays.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:亚急性硬化性全脑炎(亚急性硬化性全脑炎,SSPE)是一种由中枢神经系统持续性异常感染引起的致命性进行性神经退行性疾病。其临床特征包括认知功能减退、行为异常、进行性运动功能障碍以及刻板的慢肌阵挛抽搐,这些特征与经典的脑电图(EEG)周期性慢波复合体(Radermecker复合体)密切相关。病例报告:我们报告了SSPE的四个不同临床表现。病例1描述了一位20岁男性,最初表现为局灶性肌阵挛发作、不对称性偏瘫、认知功能下降,随后发展为全身性肌阵挛,并在鞘内注射α-干扰素治疗后出现典型的全身性Radermecker复合体。病例2展示了一位未接种疫苗的10岁男孩,表现为典型的学业成绩下降、显著的轴向和近端肢体慢肌阵挛、步态障碍以及刻板的高电压周期性慢波复合体。病例3描述了一位18岁女性,其病史为需要手术减压的脑积水,表现为学业成绩下降、周期性慢波放电以及慢肌阵挛。病例4描述了一位20岁男性,其病程为不典型且持续十年,最初被误诊为原发性精神疾病和运动障碍,之后出现严重认知功能障碍、步态停止以及典型的周期性放电。讨论与结论:这些病例展示了SSPE广泛的表型谱,包括经典的儿童期表现、局灶性发作、神经外科干扰因素以及长期精神-锥体外系伪装表现。脑电图仍然是实时神经生理学生物标志物的关键。早期临床-电生理怀疑是避免灾难性诊断延迟的必要条件。

papers.full_text: Abstract Background Measles remains a public health concern in Malaysia despite high reported vaccine coverage. Molecular surveillance is essential to distinguish endemic persistence from repeated importations and to identify immunity gaps. This study characterized the molecular epidemiology of measles virus (MeV) circulating in Malaysia from 2018 to 2024 and assessed whether the observed molecular patterns were compatible with endemic persistence or repeated introductions. Methods A total of 1,110 MeV sequences collected nationwide between 2018 and 2024 from routine surveillance and outbreak investigations were analysed alongside 28 World Health Organization reference strains. Partial N-gene (N450) sequences were genotyped using the WHO classification framework. Temporal genotype trends were assessed using logistic regression, genotype distributions were compared using χ2 tests, and phylogenetic analyses were performed using the Nextstrain Augur pipeline. Vaccination status and demographic metadata were examined to identify epidemiological patterns. Results Genotype D8 predominated throughout the study period (94%, n = 1,043), followed by B3 (4%) and genotype A (vaccine-associated) accounted for 2% of detections. Phylogenetic and molecular clock analyses showed that D8 sequences formed a highly conserved lineage (99.2–99.9% nucleotide identity). The presence of multiple phylogenetic distinct clusters across the study period was compatible with repeated introductions followed by local amplification. The odds of D8 detection increased nearly fourfold per year (p < 0.0001). Within the sequenced dataset, D8 was first detected in Terengganu in 2018, with increased representation in Sabah during 2023–2024 and phylogeographic patterns compatible with inter-regional spread involving Sabah and Peninsular Malaysia. Most cases occurred among unvaccinated children and adolescents, while 29% of sequenced cases occurred in previously vaccinated individuals. Conclusion MeV genotype D8 predominated in Malaysia from 2018 to 2024. The observed molecular and phylogenetic patterns were compatible with repeated introductions followed by local amplification, although uninterrupted low-level domestic transmission could not be excluded. analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the molecular epidemiology of measles virus (MeV) in Malaysia from 2018 to 2024, focusing on genotype D8, which predominated throughout the period. The analysis of 1,110 sequences revealed a highly conserved lineage of D8 with 99.2–99.9% nucleotide identity. However, the findings are based on sequence data and statistical trends, limiting the strength of the evidence to moderate.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 尽管高报告的疫苗覆盖率,麻疹仍然是马来西亚的公共卫生问题。本研究旨在描述2018年至2024年间在马来西亚流行的麻疹病毒(MeV)的分子流行病学。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 共计1,110个MeV序列在全国范围内于2018年至2024年间从常规的监测和暴发调查中收集,与28个世界卫生组织参考株一起进行了分析。本研究重点分析了麻疹病毒序列,并检查了疫苗接种的状态和人口统计数据,以识别流行病学模式。
elements_zh.methods: 利用世界卫生组织分类框架对部分N基因(N450)序列进行了基因分型。使用逻辑回归分析评估了基因型的时间趋势,使用χ2检验比较了基因型分布,并使用Nextstrain Augur管道进行了系统发育分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 在整个研究期间,D8型占主导地位(94%,n = 1,043),其次是B3型(4%),而A型(与疫苗相关)占检测的2%。系统发育分析和分子钟分析显示,D8序列形成了一个高度保守的谱系(核苷酸同源性为99.2–99.9%)。D8检测的几率每年几乎增加四倍(p < 0.0001)。在整个研究期间存在多个系统发育上不同的簇,这与反复引入后本地传播相一致。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 观察到的分子和系统发育模式与反复引入后本地放大相一致,尽管不能排除持续的低水平国内传播。该研究提供了对马来西亚麻疹病毒遗传动态的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现强调了分子 监测 在理解 麻疹病毒 流行和识别免疫缺口方面的重要性。它们为马来西亚 麻疹 的防控策略提供了信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于常规 监测 数据,未包含直接的因果证据。证据等级中等,因为其基于序列分析和统计趋势,而没有实验干预。

analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于常规 监测 数据,未包含直接的因果证据。证据等级中等,因为其基于序列分析和统计趋势,而没有实验干预。

papers.full_text: Abstract Nigeria’s planned Measles–Rubella (MR) vaccine rollout in October 2025 presents both a public health opportunity and an implementation challenge, particularly in addressing vaccine hesitancy and ensuring equitable uptake. This presentation examines the application of a Triple Helix collaboration model involving the Medical Women’s Association of Nigeria (MWAN) representing academia and professional practice, the Gates Foundation as an industry and development partner, and the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) as the government policy and implementation authority. Using stakeholder engagement and structured advocacy as the core methodological approach, MWAN facilitated high-level dialogue and demand-generation activities during its Biennial General Conference in Kaduna. A moderated panel session engaged public health experts, health reform advocates, and government leadership to interrogate lessons from previous immunisation campaigns (including Polio, HPV, and routine immunisation), strategies for grassroots mobilisation, health system readiness, accountability mechanisms, and monitoring frameworks for MR vaccine introduction. Data from the engagement were analysed thematically to distil lessons for collaborative vaccine advocacy. The engagement generated strong intersectoral commitment to a coordinated framework for MR advocacy, demand generation, and monitoring. Key outcomes included consensus on evidence-based, gender-responsive advocacy strategies; deployment of MWAN’s national and subnational networks for grassroots mobilisation; government reaffirmation of equitable access strategies for hard-to-reach populations; and endorsement of sustained digital and community engagement to counter misinformation. A post-conference action plan was agreed, involving multi-stakeholder technical working groups to track implementation progress ahead of the national rollout. This work demonstrates the practical value of Triple Helix collaboration in strengthening vaccine uptake and public trust. It underscores the need for deeper university–industry–government partnerships in health innovation and calls for further research to evaluate impact and scalability across immunisation programmes. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the practical value of the Triple Helix collaboration model in strengthening measles vaccine uptake and public trust, particularly in addressing vaccine hesitancy and ensuring equitable access.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a national vaccine introduction program in Nigeria, focusing on the planned Measles–Rubella (MR) vaccine rollout in October 2025. It examined the application of a Triple Helix model with stakeholder engagement and structured advocacy as the core methodological approach.
analysis.methods: Stakeholder engagement and structured advocacy were used to facilitate high-level dialogue and demand-generation activities during the Biennial General Conference in Kaduna. Data from the engagement were analysed thematically to distil lessons for collaborative vaccine advocacy.
analysis.main_results: The engagement generated strong intersectoral commitment to a coordinated framework for MR vaccine advocacy, demand generation, and monitoring. Key outcomes included consensus on evidence-based, gender-responsive advocacy strategies and deployment of MWAN’s national and subnational networks for grassroots mobilisation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the practical value of Triple Helix collaboration in strengthening vaccine uptake and public trust. They highlighted the need for deeper university–industry–government partnerships in health innovation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform collaborative vaccine advocacy strategies, demand generation, and monitoring frameworks for measles and rubella vaccination campaigns. They underscore the importance of multi-stakeholder engagement in addressing vaccine hesitancy and ensuring equitable access.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a single event, the Biennial General Conference in Kaduna, and does not include quantitative data or long-term follow-up. The evidence is moderate as it relies on thematic analysis of stakeholder engagement rather than empirical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the application of a Triple Helix collaboration model in Nigeria's planned Measles–Rubella (MR) vaccine rollout, focusing on addressing vaccine hesitancy and ensuring equitable access. The model involves the Medical Women’s Association of Nigeria (MWAN), the Gates Foundation, and the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA). Stakeholder engagement and structured advocacy were used to facilitate high-level dialogue and demand-generation activities during the Biennial General Conference in Kaduna. Thematic analysis of the engagement data revealed strong intersectoral commitment to a coordinated framework for MR vaccine advocacy, demand generation, and monitoring. The study highlights the practical value of Triple Helix collaboration in strengthening vaccine uptake and public trust, emphasizing the need for deeper university–industry–government partnerships in health innovation. However, the study is limited to a single event and lacks quantitative data or long-term follow-up, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨三螺旋合作模型在增强疫苗接种率和公众信任方面的实际价值,特别是在应对疫苗接种犹豫和确保公平接种方面。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及尼日利亚全国范围内的疫苗接种计划,重点关注计划于2025年10月开展的麻疹-风疹(MR)疫苗接种计划。研究考察了三螺旋模型的应用,该模型以利益相关者参与和结构化倡导为核心方法论。
elements_zh.methods: 通过利益相关者参与和结构化倡导,促成了卡杜纳两年一度全体大会期间的高层对话和需求生成活动。对参与活动的数据进行了主题分析,以提炼协作疫苗接种倡导的经验。
elements_zh.main_results: 参与活动产生了跨部门的强烈承诺,以建立协调的MR疫苗接种倡导、需求生成和监测框架。主要成果包括对基于证据、性别敏感的倡导策略达成共识,并部署了MWAN的全国和地方网络进行基层动员。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将研究结果解释为表明三螺旋合作在增强疫苗接种率和公众信任方面的实际价值。他们强调了在卫生创新中深化大学-产业-政府伙伴关系的必要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为协作疫苗接种倡导策略、需求生成以及MR疫苗接种计划的监测框架提供参考。它们突显了多利益相关者参与在应对疫苗接种犹豫和确保公平接种方面的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究基于卡杜纳两年一度全体大会这一单一事件,未包含定量数据或长期随访。证据强度中等,因为它依赖于对利益相关者参与的主题分析,而非实证数据。

papers.title: Multi-pathogen serosurveillance reveals correlated vaccination performance, waning tetanus immunity, and diphtheria boosting in Zambian children.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Vaccination coverage estimates and case-based surveillance have limitations in evaluating immunization programs. Serosurveillance offers a complementary approach by directly measuring population immunity. We assessed whether serologic analyses across multiple antigens (i.e., measles, diphtheria, tetanus) could provide additional insights into vaccination program performance. METHODS: We conducted a matched case-control study among children aged 2- to 10-years-old (n = 1286) in Zambia using specimens from the 2016 ZAMPHIA survey. Using previously generated data on measles serostatus, measles seronegative children (i.e., "cases") were matched to measles seropositive children (i.e., "controls") on sex, age, HIV infection status, and province. Samples were tested for tetanus and diphtheria antitoxin IgG antibodies using commercial enzyme immunoassays. We estimated the odds of tetanus and diphtheria seropositivity by measles serostatus using conditional logistic regression and examined age-specific antibody dynamics. RESULTS: Measles seronegative children had 1.7-fold increased odds (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.3-2.1) of being tetanus seronegative compared to measles seropositive children. Diphtheria serostatus had no significant association with measles serostatus (odds ratio: 1.3; 95% CrI: 0.9-1.7). Tetanus seroprevalence declined monotonically with age. However, diphtheria seroprevalence initially declined through 5 years of age, then increased again beginning at 6 years of age despite the lack of vaccine booster doses given after the primary series in infancy, potentially from asymptomatic or subclinical infections. CONCLUSIONS: Serologic analyses revealed measles serostatus was positively associated with tetanus serostatus (where seropositivity arises only via vaccination and not infection), suggesting children who are measles seronegative are more likely to have missed DTP vaccination. We additionally found that measles serostatus was not associated with diphtheria serostatus, suggesting that antibody responses to diphtheria continue to boost beyond infancy when DTP vaccination is given. Our findings support consideration of DTP booster doses in Zambia to address waning tetanus immunity and further investigation of potential diphtheria carriage and transmission.

analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a matched case-control study among children aged 2- to 10-years-old (n = 1286) in Zambia using specimens from the 2016 ZAMPHIA survey.
analysis.methods: Measles seronegative children (i.e., "cases") were matched to measles seropositive children (i.e., "controls") on sex, age, HIV infection status, and province. Samples were tested for tetanus and diphtheria antitoxin IgG antibodies using commercial enzyme immunoassays. We estimated the odds of tetanus and diphtheria seropositivity by measles serostatus using conditional logistic regression and examined age-specific antibody dynamics.
analysis.main_results: Measles seronegative children had 1.7-fold increased odds (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.3-2.1) of being tetanus seronegative compared to measles seropositive children. Tetanus seroprevalence declined monotonically with age. Diphtheria serostatus had no significant association with measles serostatus (odds ratio: 1.3; 95% CrI: 0.9-1.7).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Serologic analyses revealed measles serostatus was positively associated with tetanus serostatus (where seropositivity arises only via vaccination and not infection), suggesting children who are measles seronegative are more likely to have missed DTP vaccination.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: We additionally found that measles serostatus was not associated with diphtheria serostatus, suggesting that antibody responses to diphtheria continue to boost beyond infancy when DTP vaccination is given.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Our findings support consideration of DTP booster doses in Zambia to address waning tetanus immunity and further investigation of potential diphtheria carriage and transmission.

analysis.summary_en: This study used serosurveillance to evaluate vaccination program performance in Zambian children by analyzing measles, tetanus, and diphtheria immunity. The research aimed to determine whether serologic analyses could provide additional insights into immunization effectiveness. A matched case-control study was conducted among 1286 children aged 2- to 10-years-old using specimens from the 2016 ZAMPHIA survey. Measles seronegative children had 1.7-fold increased odds of being tetanus seronegative compared to measles seropositive children, indicating a possible link between measles serostatus and DTP vaccination status. Tetanus seroprevalence decreased with age, while diphtheria serostatus showed no significant association with measles serostatus. The authors suggest that DTP booster doses may be necessary to address waning tetanus immunity and that diphtheria antibody responses may continue to boost beyond infancy. The study highlights the value of serosurveillance in understanding immunization program performance and the dynamics of immunity in children.

papers.title_zh: 多病原体血清学监测揭示了疫苗接种表现的相关性、破伤风免疫力减弱以及在赞比亚儿童中白喉抗体增强
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Vaccination coverage estimates and case-based surveillance have limitations in evaluating immunization programs. Serosurveillance offers a complementary approach by directly measuring population immunity. We assessed whether serologic analyses across multiple antigens (i.e., measles, diphtheria, tetanus) could provide additional insights into vaccination program performance. METHODS: We conducted a matched case-control study among children aged 2- to 10-years-old (n = 1286) in Zambia using specimens from the 2016 ZAMPHIA survey. Using previously generated data on measles serostatus, measles seronegative children (i.e., "cases") were matched to measles seropositive children (i.e., "controls") on sex, age, HIV infection status, and province. Samples were tested for tetanus and diphtheria antitoxin IgG antibodies using commercial enzyme immunoassays. We estimated the odds of tetanus and diphtheria seropositivity by measles serostatus using conditional logistic regression and examined age-specific antibody dynamics. RESULTS: Measles seronegative children had 1.7-fold increased odds (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.3-2.1) of being tetanus seronegative compared to measles seropositive children. Diphtheria serostatus had no significant association with measles serostatus (odds ratio: 1.3; 95% CrI: 0.9-1.7). Tetanus seroprevalence declined monotonically with age. However, diphtheria seroprevalence initially declined through 5 years of age, then increased again beginning at 6 years of age despite the lack of vaccine booster doses given after the primary series in infancy, potentially from asymptomatic or subclinical infections. CONCLUSIONS: Serologic analyses revealed measles serostatus was positively associated with tetanus serostatus (where seropositivity arises only via vaccination and not infection), suggesting children who are measles seronegative are more likely to have missed DTP vaccination. We additionally found that measles serostatus was not associated with diphtheria serostatus, suggesting that antibody responses to diphtheria continue to boost beyond infancy when DTP vaccination is given. Our findings support consideration of DTP booster doses in Zambia to address waning tetanus immunity and further investigation of potential diphtheria carriage and transmission.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:疫苗接种覆盖率估计和基于病例的监测存在局限性,难以评估免疫接种计划。血清学监测通过直接测量人群免疫力提供了一种补充方法。我们评估了通过多种抗原(即麻疹、白喉、破伤风)的血清学分析是否能为疫苗接种计划的表现提供额外见解。方法:我们使用2016年ZAMPHIA调查的样本,在赞比亚对2至10岁儿童(n = 1286)进行了匹配的病例对照研究。基于之前生成的麻疹血清状态数据,我们将麻疹血清阴性儿童(即“病例”)与麻疹血清阳性儿童(即“对照”)按性别、年龄、HIV感染状态和省份进行匹配。使用商业酶免疫测定法检测破伤风和白喉抗毒素IgG抗体。我们采用条件逻辑回归估计麻疹血清状态对破伤风和白喉血清阳性率的比值,并分析年龄特异性抗体动态。结果:与麻疹血清阳性儿童相比,麻疹血清阴性儿童出现破伤风血清阴性的可能性增加了1.7倍(95%可信区间[CrI]:1.3-2.1)。白喉血清状态与麻疹血清状态无显著关联(比值比:1.3;95% CrI:0.9-1.7)。破伤风血清流行率随年龄单调下降。然而,白喉血清流行率在5岁前下降,随后在6岁开始再次上升,尽管在婴儿期完成基础系列后未给予疫苗加强剂,这可能源于无症状或亚临床感染。结论:血清学分析显示麻疹血清状态与破伤风血清状态呈正相关(其中血清阳性仅通过疫苗接种产生,而非感染),表明麻疹血清阴性儿童更可能错过了DTP 疫苗接种。我们还发现麻疹血清状态与白喉血清状态无关联,这表明当给予DTP 疫苗接种时,白喉的免疫应答可能在婴儿期后继续增强。我们的研究结果支持在赞比亚考虑DTP加强剂以应对破伤风免疫力减弱,并进一步研究潜在的白喉携带状态和传播。

Services Departments Home News Flash Public Health Reminds Residents to Protect Themselves Against Measles and Seasonal Illnesses News Flash Public Health Reminds Residents to Protect Themselves Against Measles and Seasonal Illnesses Maricopa County Department of Public Health (MCDPH) has confirmed one new public exposure site for measles as the result of a travel-associated measles case in a Maricopa County resident. This exposure comes as seasonal, vaccine-preventable diseases are on the rise. “Measles is making headlines, but we have several illnesses spreading right now, and we have vaccines to protect against many of them, including measles,” said Dr. Nick Staab, chief medical officer for MCDPH. “While it can sound alarming, the good news is that there are steps we can all take to protect ourselves and those around us.” What residents and visitors can do There are several steps people can take to protect themselves and their loved ones. Protect yourself with the measles vaccine Measles vaccines are available year-round for those who are not up-to-date. An early dose is currently recommended for infants ages 6-11 months to protect them against the higher potential for exposure. This year, there have been 28 cases of measles reported in Maricopa County and more than 3,000 cases in the U.S. Get seasonal respiratory vaccines in early fall Updated vaccines for seasonal flu, COVID-19, and RSV are available now for the upcoming respiratory virus season. COVID-19 cases are already increasing, so now is the time to get protected. Getting protected against seasonal respiratory viruses by the end of October helps the body build its immunity in time for end-of-year holidays and gatherings. Learn to recognize symptoms and what to do if you get them Fever, chills, body aches, coughs, and congestion are common symptoms of viruses. If you develop symptoms, stay home and away from others to prevent spreading germs. Seek healthcare if you are at higher risk of complications or your symptoms are concerning. Why prevention matters Sickness from preventable illnesses cause many impacts within our community. Some of them include: Lost days of learning for kids who have to stay home Lost wages for people who are sick or need to stay home with sick family members More hospital visits for preventable illnesses, which reduces the number of hospital beds and staff available for issues like accidents, heart attacks, and other emergencies Avoid long-term impacts: Some viruses can cause long-term health risks. For example, measles infection can lead to a dangerous brain-swelling condition several years after a person recovers from their initial infection. Similarly, varicella infection (also known as chickenpox) can lead to shingles later in life, a painful complication that can be avoided with the varicella vaccine or, if you’ve already had varicella, with the shingles vaccine. Common respiratory viruses can develop into complicated pneumonias, hospitalizations, and death. Protect those at higher risk: Young infants are too young to be vaccinated against flu, measles, and other viruses. They depend on the people around them to reduce their chances of being exposed to these viruses and becoming sick. The same applies for people who are undergoing cancer treatments, who have had organ transplants, and many other conditions. “Lots of medical risk factors are invisible, so you might never know that you’re around people who are at higher risk of hospitalization or complications from these illnesses,” said Dr. Staab. “By taking these simple preventive steps, we can reduce the chances of serious sickness for our friends and neighbors, and we can keep our own families from losing time at school and work due to sickness.” Public exposure to measles Public notifications are issued when exposed individuals cannot be identified, so people who may have been in a public setting at the same time as an infectious person can learn of their potential exposure and take protective steps. MCDPH will provide public notification via the media and update its online list of public exposure sites when public exposures are identified. People who were at the following location at the listed date and time may have been exposed to measles and should watch for symptoms. The measles virus can survive in the air for up to two hours, and the listed exposure times include that extended period. Location Date/Time Time Watch for symptoms through this date NEW Walgreens 11250 E. Via Linda Scottsdale, 85259 Tuesday, September 8 8:00 a.m.–10:25 a.m. Tuesday, September 29 People who were at the locations during the listed dates and times should: Check your vaccination status. Review your immunization records to confirm you are protected against measles. People who have not had measles or received the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine may not be protected and should talk with a healthcare provider about vaccination. If you are not protected against measles, the MMR vaccine is safe and the most effective way to prevent measles infections. Watch for symptoms, which typically appear seven to 12 days after exposure but may take up to 21 days. Symptoms include: High fever (> 101°F) Red, watery eyes Cough Runny nose A rash that is red, raised, and blotchy. The rash begins after other symptoms, usually on the face at the hairline, and moves down the body. View photos of measles. In some situations, certain people exposed to measles may be eligible for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to reduce their risk of becoming ill. This includes some children under 12 months, pregnant women, and individuals with compromised immune systems. Individuals should contact their healthcare provider for guidance. If symptoms develop, stay at home, and call a healthcare provider to seek medical care and testing. Call ahead and let them know about your symptoms and possible measles exposure so you can be seen without exposing others. For more information on measles, visit Maricopa.gov/measles. For more information on seasonal viruses, visit Maricopa.gov/fallwinter. ### Media contact: Sonia Singh, Sonia.singh@maricopa.gov, 602-679-3098 Back to Top Loading Loading Close × Opens in new window PDF Download Word Download Excel Download PowerPoint Download Document Download

analysis.brief_en: Maricopa County Department of Public Health (MCDPH) has confirmed a measles exposure linked to a travel-associated case in a local resident. The exposure occurred at a Walgreens location in Scottsdale on September 8, 2026, from 8:00 a.m. to 10:25 a.m., and individuals present during this time are advised to monitor for symptoms through September 29, 2026. This year, 28 measles cases have been reported in Maricopa County, with over 3,000 cases nationwide. MCDPH is issuing public notifications through media and its online list of exposure sites. Those not vaccinated or immune are encouraged to consult healthcare providers about the MMR vaccine. Symptoms of measles include high fever, red eyes, cough, runny nose, and a rash that typically appears seven to 12 days after exposure. The measles virus can survive in the air for up to two hours and may lead to severe complications, such as brain swelling, years after infection. MCDPH emphasizes the importance of vaccination to protect individuals, especially young infants and those with compromised immune systems, who are more vulnerable to the virus. The notice serves as a reminder to residents and visitors to take preventive measures against measles and other seasonal illnesses.

news.title_zh: 公共卫生提醒居民防范麻疹和季节性疾病 - 马里科帕县(.gov)
news.source_body_en: Maricopa County Department of Public Health (MCDPH) has confirmed a measles exposure linked to a travel-associated case in a local resident. news.content_zh: 马里科帕县公共卫生部(MCDPH)已确认一名当地居民与旅行相关病例有关的麻疹暴露。该暴露发生在2026年9月8日,地点为斯科茨代尔的沃尔格林药店,时间为上午8:00至上午10:25。在此期间内到场的人员应监测症状至2026年9月29日。今年,马里科帕县报告了28例麻疹病例,全国范围内超过3000例。MCDPH通过媒体和其在线暴露地点列表发布公共通知。未接种疫苗或免疫力低下的人群被鼓励咨询医疗提供者关于MMR疫苗的情况。麻疹的症状包括高热、红眼、咳嗽、流鼻涕和通常在暴露后7至12天出现的皮疹。麻疹病毒可以在空气中存活长达两小时,感染后可能导致严重的并发症,如脑水肿,甚至多年后。MCDPH强调疫苗接种的重要性,以保护尤其是年幼的婴儿和免疫系统受损的人群,他们更容易受到病毒的影响。通知提醒居民和访客采取预防措施以防范麻疹和其他季节性疾病。

Cancel Translate Home The latest news + events Press releases Health Department Warns of Possible Measles Exposure at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Send via email Print this page Health Department Warns of Possible Measles Exposure at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) For immediate release: September 17, 2026Published by: Department of Public Health Contact: James Garrow phlpublichealth@phila.gov PHILADELPHIA—The Philadelphia Department of Public Health (PDPH) is notifying the public of a probable measles exposure at CHOP, 3401 Civic Center Boulevard, Philadelphia, PA 19104, on Friday, September 11, 2026, at the following locations and times within the hospital. CHOP NICU West: 9:30 am to 4:15 pm CHOP NICU West Family Lounge: 9:30 am to 4:15 pm CHOP Atrium: 9:30 am to 4:15 pm CHOP Main Cafeteria: 12:05 pm – 2:45 pm CHOP, the Pennsylvania Department of Health, and PDPH are working closely to ensure potentially exposed infants receive a preventative antibody product to prevent or lessen severe disease and to take steps to prevent the further spread of measles. PDPH is encouraging people who were exposed to check their vaccination status and watch for symptoms. Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air when infected people cough, sneeze, or talk. People who aren’t protected against measles can get the virus up to two hours after someone else with measles left the same room or airspace. The early symptoms of measles are fever, runny nose, cough, and red, watery eyes, followed by rash. In some people, it can be a very serious infection that leads to pneumonia, brain infection, and death. “We encourage people to get vaccinated not only to protect themselves, but to protect those who cannot get vaccinated. This is why it is imperative that everyone who is eligible gets up to date on the vaccines they need so we can protect our most vulnerable,” said Health Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson. “We do not believe that these exposures constitute a broad risk to Philadelphians, since the vast majority of us are fully protected due to our being vaccinated. Given the ongoing outbreaks in Pennsylvania and other places, it is imperative that everyone who is not up to date on their MMR vaccine gets their vaccine as soon as possible. Remember, this is not just about protecting yourself, it’s about protecting our most vulnerable Philadelphians.” The MMR vaccine is safe and highly effective and is the best way to avoid serious complications of a vaccine-preventable disease. MMR vaccine is routinely recommended for patients 12–15 months with a second dose given at age 4–6 years. Infants under 12 months are not routinely eligible for the vaccine and are not protected. An early first dose of MMR (dose 0) is recommended for infants 6–11 months of age before travel to areas with measles, including Lancaster, Lebanon, Berks, Dauphin, Northumberland, and York counties in PA. Any child with planned international travel should also receive an early dose of MMR. An early second dose of MMR should be given to children 12 months through 4 years before they travel to areas with measles, including parts of PA, as well as before any international travel and at least 28 days after the previous dose. To learn where you can get a vaccine, please visit phila.gov/measles. The Health Department recommends the following: Anyone possibly exposed to the measles case should follow the steps below to determine if you are protected from measles, and symptoms to look out for if you are not protected. Determine if you are protected against measles. Generally, you are considered protected (immune) if you were: Born before 1957, or Have already had measles, or Have received two doses of measles-containing vaccine (usually given as measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine). Look at your vaccination records or ask your healthcare provider to see if you have already had two doses of this vaccine. If you have only received one dose of measles-containing vaccine, your risk of measles following this exposure is low. Discuss getting the second dose of the vaccine with your healthcare provider. If you are protected from measles, you do not have to do anything. MMR vaccines are extremely effective at preventing measles. If you are not protected from measles, you should receive a dose of MMR vaccine. Talk to your healthcare provider to learn how you can get this vaccine. Those who are under 12 months of age, pregnant and not immune, or are immunosuppressed (have a weakened immune system) should consult with their healthcare provider as soon as possible. Management of exposure to measles may be different with these conditions. Measles is contagious for 4 days before to 4 days after rash starts. If you are not immune and may have been exposed, you could give measles to someone at high risk before developing rash. To prevent that from happening, please wear a mask in indoor public spaces and around anyone who is unvaccinated until 3 weeks after the exposure. If you are not immune and may have been exposed, and you develop any symptoms through October 2, 2026 that appear like measles, contact your doctor immediately. The early symptoms of measles are fever, runny nose, cough, and red, watery eyes, followed by rash. Tell your doctor that you may have been exposed to measles. You should also notify your local health department (Philadelphia: 215-685-6740) or the state health department at 877-724-3258 for residents of other counties in Pennsylvania if you develop measles symptoms. For more information about measles, visit the CDC’s webpage on measles. The Health Department will post any updates on exposures on phila.gov/measles as needed. ### Press Releases Press Release Health Department Warns of Possible Measles Exposure at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) September 17, 2026 Press Release Philadelphia Department of Public Health Releases Comprehensive Maternal Mortality Report Covering 2019-2023 September 15, 2026 Press Release Health Department to Spray for Mosquitoes in Fairmount September 6, 2026 Press Release El Departamento de Sanidad pulverizará contra los mosquitos en Fairmount September 6, 2026 See all Press releases Top Search for: Birth, marriage & life events Business & self-employment Cars, parking & transportation Crime, law & justice Culture & recreation Diversity, inclusion, accessibility & immigration Education & learning Ethics & transparency Mental & physical health Payments, assistance & taxes Permits, violations & licenses Property, lots & housing Safety & emergency preparedness Streets, sidewalks & alleys Trash, recycling & city upkeep Trees, parks & the environment Water, gas & utilities Working & jobs Zoning, planning & development

analysis_en.time: Cancel Translate Home The latest news + events Press releases Health Department Warns of Possible Measles Exposure at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Send via email Print this page Health Department Warns of Possible Measles Exposure at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) For immediate release: September 17, 2026Published by: Department of Public Health Contact: James Garrow phlpublichealth@phila.gov PHILADELPHIA—The Philadelphia Department of Public Health (PDPH) is notifying the public of a probable measles exposure at CHOP, 3401 Civic Center Boulevard, Philadelphia, PA 19104, on Friday, September 11, 2026, at the following locations and times within the hospital.
analysis_en.location_and_population: In some people, it can be a very serious infection that leads to pneumonia, brain infection, and death.
analysis_en.event: The Health Department recommends the following: Anyone possibly exposed to the measles case should follow the steps below to determine if you are protected from measles, and symptoms to look out for if you are not protected.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: Generally, you are considered protected (immune) if you were: Born before 1957, or Have already had measles, or Have received two doses of measles-containing vaccine (usually given as measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine).
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: An early first dose of MMR (dose 0) is recommended for infants 6–11 months of age before travel to areas with measles, including Lancaster, Lebanon, Berks, Dauphin, Northumberland, and York counties in PA.

Vaccines See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Measles is an extremely contagious virus, but deaths have been rare in the United States due to high rates of vaccination. Centers for Disease Control A fourth person with measles has died in Pennsylvania, the state announced Tuesday — marking the first time in decades the United States has recorded so many deaths in a single year. Measles deaths have been extremely rare in the United States because most people are protected by a highly effective vaccine. But as vaccination rates decline nationally and measles cases rise globally, experts say the death toll from measles may continue to grow in the United States this year and beyond. How common are measles deaths in the United States? The last year with at least four measles deaths in the United States was 1992. Ad Feedback Until the recent resurgence in cases, the United States went several years without any measles deaths. Last year, there were three measles deaths, and before then, the last measles death was in 2015, when a Washington state woman died. Before then, the United States hadn’t had a measles death since 2003. Related article This Electron Micrograph Reveals Both A Paramyxovirus Measles Virus, And Virions Of The Polyomavirus, Simian Virus Sv40 Smaller Circles. The Envelope Of The Measles Virus Has Broken, Exposing The Nucleocapsid Filaments. Interest In Sv40 Has Increased In The Last Several Years Because The Virus Was Found In Certain Forms Of Cancer In Humans, For Instance Mesotheliomas Rare Tumors Located In The Lungs, Brain, And Bone Tumors Carbone Et Al. , 1994; Jasani Et Al. , 2001. (Photo By BSIP/UIG Via Getty Images) BSIP/UIG via Getty Images Pennsylvania reports fourth measles-related death, the most in US in decades 4 min read This year was already the second record-breaking year in a row for measles cases. As of July, the country has recorded more measles cases than in any other year since 1991. Before the vaccine became available in 1963, measles sickened 3 million to 4 million people and led to about 500 deaths every year in the United States. Measles was declared eliminated from the United States in 2000, but recent outbreaks mean that status will be reassessed in November. In a Tuesday Senate hearing, the nominee for deputy secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, Chris Klomp, appeared to acknowledge the US had lost its elimination status, and endorsed measles vaccination strongly as the best way to regain it. “Unquestionably, the MMR [measles, mumps, rubella] vaccine is the single most effective public health tool that we have against measles,” Klomp, a former healthcare executive, told the Senate Finance Committee in the first of two confirmation hearings over two days. “It’s 97% effective after two doses to preventing transmission, and is the single best thing that we can do to eradicate and establish our exemption from measles again.” How common are measles deaths globally? Measles deaths are much more common in low-income countries with weaker health infrastructure than in the United States or similar countries. Globally, an estimated 95,000 people died from measles in 2024, according to the World Health Organization. Ninety-five percent of those deaths were in low-income countries. Measles is considered the most contagious infectious disease known to humans; up to 9 out of 10 unvaccinated people who come in contact with an infected person will catch the virus. Vaccinations have proven highly successful, preventing an estimated 59 million deaths from 2000 to 2024, WHO said. Before widespread vaccination, measles caused an estimated 2.6 million deaths globally each year. Other high-income countries have seen record numbers of measles cases in recent years as well; last year, Canada reported 5,462 measles cases and two deaths. The country lost its elimination status because of sustained transmission for more than a year, a fact HHS nominee Klomp pointed out. Many countries have lost their elimination status, Klomp told Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon and the ranking member of the finance committee. “We’ve seen vaccination rates dropping all over the world, not just the United States,” Klomp said. Nonetheless, Klomp’s unequivocal embrace of the MMR vaccine contrasted with the mixed messaging from his boss, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic who has downplayed the seriousness of measles. Related video CNN Trump’s new CDC Director excludes PA deaths from measles update 3:21 Is this number of deaths unexpected? Globally, measles typically kills nearly 3 out of every 1,000 people who get sick; in the United States, it’s about 1 in 1,000, research shows. As of this week, Pennsylvania had counted at least 693 measles cases, 133 hospitalizations and four deaths, according to the Pennsylvania health department. The official tally is likely an undercount. Measles cases are often unreported when people have milder symptoms and don’t see a doctor who would report the case. Pennsylvania’s death toll is “on the high side,” said Johns Hopkins University Professor Dr. William Moss, an epidemiologist who has studied measles for years. Moss believes the higher number of deaths in Pennsylvania “reflects the fact that these infections occurred in individuals, except for the 18-year-old, with underlying risk factors for severe illness and mortality, particularly the two infants.” One infant who died had a ruptured spleen and died shortly after birth. The other infant had Amish microcephaly, a rare and severe genetic disorder that causes a small head and underdeveloped brain and leaves children with little chance of surviving beyond a couple of months, Moss said. The 40-year-old woman who died had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which increased her risk for a severe lung infection from measles. “They’re all tragic cases, all unvaccinated cases, but kind of unique in their underlying risk factors for severe measles,” Moss said. What is acute disseminated encephalomyelitis? The Mifflin County, Pennsylvania, coroner said this week that an 18-year-old with measles died from acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, known as ADEM. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is a severe neurological complication of measles that triggers rapid inflammation and swelling in the brain and spinal cord. It develops in about 1 in 1,000 measles cases. “It’s just a relatively rare, but known complication of measles that can occur in anyone, even otherwise healthy individuals,” Moss said. Could there be something new or worse about the virus circulating now? Neither Moss nor Dr. David Margolius, director of the Cleveland Department of Health, believes the virus has mutated to become more deadly. There may be more deaths because there are more cases and fewer people are getting vaccinated, Margolius said. “So it’s been given a door in, and it’s taken advantage and the virus has spread across many populations across the world,” Margolius said. Related vertical video CBS Dr. Oz: MMR vaccine is not ‘lethal’ Are vaccinated people at risk of death from measles? Measles vaccination is very safe and highly effective, providing lifelong protection for most people. Joe Raedle/Getty Images There is no specific treatment for measles, so prevention is the best way to reduce risk of serious illness or death. The measles vaccine is highly effective, providing 97% protection for most people. “It’s not perfect and we have a two-dose vaccine schedule for a reason,” Moss said. “Not everyone responds to the first dose.” The risk of death from measles for vaccinated people is “very low, unless you’re immunosuppressed in some way,” Moss said. Measles, mumps and rubella protection are combined into one vaccine administered when a baby is between 12 to 15 months old. Children get a second dose between ages 4 and 6. For most people, protection provided by the vaccine lasts a lifetime. Who’s most at risk of serious illness from measles? Measles can be serious for anyone at any age, but some groups are more at risk of serious complications, including: Children younger than 5 Adults older than 20 People who are pregnant People with weakened immune systems from conditions such as HIV or leukemia Related video CNN Dr. Paul Offit: ‘No,’ the US cannot still claim to have measles elimination status 1:31 What are some of the long-term risks of measles infection? Measles is well known for its rash, fever and cough, but it can also cause seizures, blindness, deafness and permanent lung damage. Measles can also weaken the central nervous system and immune system, resulting in serious disease or death years later. The measles virus can also essentially wipe out the body’s previous immune memory, making people vulnerable to other dangerous infections, even long after they recover from the initial infection. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, is a rare but fatal central nervous system disease that can develop seven to 10 years after a person is infected and seems to have recovered. Before vaccination was widely available, about 1,000 people developed chronic disability from acute encephalitis caused by measles annually, according to the CDC. analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is monitoring the situation, and the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is re-evaluating the elimination status of measles. The article notes that the HHS nominee Chris Klomp acknowledged the loss of elimination status and endorsed vaccination as the best way to regain it. However, the article also mentions that the official tally of cases and deaths is likely an undercount due to underreporting.

news.title_zh: 美国麻疹死亡病例有多常见?随着疫苗接种率下降
news.source_body_en: CNN reported in September 2026 that the United States has seen a resurgence in measles cases, with the fourth measles-related death in Pennsylvania marking the first time in decades that the country has recorded multiple deaths in a single year. The article highlights that measles deaths have been rare in the US due to high vaccination rates, but the risk is increasing as rates decline. Globally, an estimated 95,000 people died from measles in 2024, with 95% of those deaths occurring in low-income countries. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is monitoring the situation, and the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is re-evaluating the elimination status of measles. The HHS nominee Chris Klomp acknowledged the loss of elimination status and endorsed vaccination as the best way to regain it. However, the article also mentions that the official tally of cases and deaths is likely an undercount due to underreporting. The piece emphasizes the importance of the MMR vaccine in preventing measles and its associated deaths, noting that it is 97% effective after two doses.

A measles virus under a microscope. Callista Images/Image Source/Getty Images A 40-year-old woman who lived in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, has died from measles complications, the county coroner confirmed Sunday. It’s the third measles-associated death in a fast-growing outbreak that’s sparked a political clash between state and federal officials. The woman died Saturday, according to a news release from the Jefferson County Coroner’s Office, which said it was working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on the case. The woman hadn’t been vaccinated against measles, the coroner, Greg Furlong, confirmed to CNN. The death follows two measles-associated deaths reported in Lancaster County at the end of August, the first connected to the viral illness in the state in 35 years. That county is the epicenter of Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak, which had reached 676 cases as of Friday, 108 of which were added in the previous week. One hundred twenty-four people have been hospitalized. Ad Feedback “This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said in a statement posted on the coroner’s office’s Facebook page. The woman contracted measles after a family member had it as well, Furlong told CNN, and noted she also had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, and asthma, and had been on supplemental oxygen 24 hours a day before getting measles. The state health department said it’s in touch with the coroner and is conducting its own review of the case, and said it will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available. In some of her first public comments about the country’s measles outbreaks, Dr. Erica Schwartz, the newly confirmed director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said in a statement that the agency hadn’t been notified by Pennsylvania officials of the death. “Despite repeated offers of assistance, Pennsylvania has not requested a CDC Epi-Aid, which would deploy epidemiologists and provide on-the-ground measles outbreak support,” Schwartz’s statement, shared with CNN by email, said. “By contrast, Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin have officially requested CDC Epi-Aids and worked alongside federal teams to help bring their measles outbreaks under control. CDC remains ready to provide Epi-Aid support to Pennsylvania as soon as the state officially requests our help.” Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, said in late August when the state announced the first two measles-associated deaths that he’d declined an offer from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, for federal help. He then said he’d told the secretary that his “actions and his rhetoric,” including spreading misinformation about vaccines, was harming communities. Kennedy, an outspoken vaccine skeptic, shot back on social media, accusing Shapiro of fearmongering and the “weaponization of infectious disease” for political gain. He suggested the deaths may have been “altogether fabricated” by one of Shapiro’s “hopeful staffers” to support a narrative that measles infection is more dangerous than it actually is. The two deaths in Lancaster County were in infants, the county coroner there said, but his office disputed whether one of the deaths was caused by measles. A newborn died of a ruptured spleen, which the coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said his forensic pathologist deemed wasn’t caused by the viral illness. A second death, in a six-week-old infant with a serious genetic condition called Amish lethal microcephaly, was caused by measles, Diamantoni told CNN. Callista Images/Image Source/Getty Images A 40-year-old woman who lived in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, has died from measles complications, the county coroner confirmed Sunday. It’s the third measles-associated death in a fast-growing outbreak that’s sparked a political clash between state and federal officials. That county is the epicenter of Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak, which had reached 676 cases as of Friday, 108 of which were added in the previous week. One hundred twenty-four people have been hospitalized. The woman contracted measles after a family member had it as well, Furlong told CNN, and noted she also had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, and asthma, and had been on supplemental oxygen 24 hours a day before getting measles. The state health department said it’s in touch with the coroner and is conducting its own review of the case, and said it will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available. CDC remains ready to provide Epi-Aid support to Pennsylvania as soon as the state officially requests our help.” Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, said in late August when the state announced the first two measles-associated deaths that he’d declined an offer from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, for federal help. He then said he’d told the secretary that his “actions and his rhetoric,” including spreading misinformation about vaccines, was harming communities. Kennedy, an outspoken vaccine skeptic, shot back on social media, accusing Shapiro of fearmongering and the “weaponization of infectious disease” for political gain. He suggested the deaths may have been “altogether fabricated” by one of Shapiro’s “hopeful staffers” to support a narrative that measles infection is more dangerous than it actually is. The two deaths in Lancaster County were in infants, the county coroner there said, but his office disputed whether one of the deaths was caused by measles. A newborn died of a ruptured spleen, which the coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said his forensic pathologist deemed wasn’t caused by the viral illness. A second death, in a six-week-old infant with a serious genetic condition called Amish lethal microcephaly, was caused by measles, Diamantoni told CNN. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. One of every 1,000 kids with measles will develop brain swelling. The virus kills one to three of every 1,000 children who become infected. “Many people associate measles with a childhood illness, but it can lead to severe complications in individuals of any age,” Jefferson County Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver said in the office’s statement. “Measles is highly contagious and can result in serious respiratory illness, hospitalization, and in rare cases like this, death.” The MMR vaccine is the best way to protect against measles, the CDC says. Two doses provide 97% protection against measles. Approved since 1963, the vaccine is very safe, and side effects are usually mild and go away on their own, the agency says. In its statement Sunday, the state health department reiterated that last month, it “confirmed two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania,” adding, “The Department’s primary focus remains on stopping the spread of measles across the Commonwealth by expanding access to measles vaccination.” CNN’s Brenda Goodman contributed to this report. Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Minneapolis/ Crime & Emergencies Fillmore County Confirms Measles Case as Minnesota's 2026 Count Hits 25 By Zach White Published on September 18, 2026 902 Houston St. NW #2 — County Agency Coordinating Case Response Google Street View An unvaccinated adult in Fillmore County has tested positive for measles, health officials confirmed, marking the 25th case reported in Minnesota over the past year and prompting an urgent push to trace anyone who may have been exposed. The case stems from domestic transmission, and local officials are now working to identify people who came into contact with the infected person before the highly contagious virus spreads further through southeastern Minnesota. The case was identified by the Minnesota Department of Health laboratory, according to Fillmore County Public Health, as first reported by WJON. The Minnesota Department of Health has now identified another measles case in southeast Minnesota, with three cases reported in neighboring Olmsted County over the past year. Statewide, the tally is 25 confirmed cases, compared with the 18 cases Bring Me The News reported in an earlier account, when it noted that the adult in this case contracted the virus while traveling within the United States. Fillmore County health officials are working to identify additional people who may be showing measles symptoms, which include a high fever that can exceed 104 degrees Fahrenheit, along with a runny nose, cough, red or watery eyes, and a rash. The virus spreads through the air when infected people breathe or cough, making it one of the most transmissible diseases known. Anyone displaying these symptoms is urged to stay home and avoid visitors until speaking with a doctor. How the Case Fits Into Minnesota's Year The state's official disease surveillance data tells a longer story. Minnesota recorded 26 measles cases in 2025 and had logged 18 cases in 2026 to date, according to the Minnesota Department of Health, with the vast majority tied to domestic exposures rather than international travel. That earlier 2026 count has now climbed past that mark with the Fillmore County confirmation and additional cases counted since. The department's data also tracks recent regional cases in Minnesota. The surrounding region is under heavy pressure. Southwestern Wisconsin is in the grip of a major localized outbreak, with 155 confirmed cases centered in Grant, Iowa, and Lafayette counties contributing to a statewide Wisconsin total of 163 cases in 2026, according to CIDRAP. That outbreak is near southeastern Minnesota, where Fillmore County is located, underscoring the risk of cross-border spread. Nationally, the picture is even starker: the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 3,294 confirmed measles cases across 47 U.S. jurisdictions as of September 10, 2026, compared with 2,289 cases in all of 2025, putting the country on pace for its worst measles year in more than three decades. Vaccination Gaps in Rural Minnesota Public health officials have repeatedly pointed to vaccination as the only safe way to prevent measles, and they're urging Fillmore County residents to check their vaccination status, report symptoms to a health care provider or local health department, seek testing if symptoms appear, and get vaccinated as needed. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective at preventing infection, per CDC clinical guidance. Because measles is so contagious, public health experts say roughly 95% population immunity is needed to prevent community spread. That threshold has become harder to reach in parts of rural Minnesota. Hoodline reported in earlier coverage of Menahga's kindergarten vaccination rates that the state's kindergarten measles vaccination rate has slipped below the 92.5% national average, with the weakest coverage concentrated in rural areas carrying higher rates of vaccine exemptions. That gap presents a challenge for rural residents. Echoes of a Larger 2017 Outbreak Minnesota has faced measles outbreaks before. That history remains a reminder of the risks posed by measles. Measles can cause severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis. Fast contact tracing is especially important during the virus's 10-to-21-day incubation period. That window is now the focus for Fillmore County health officials, who are racing to map every possible exposure tied to this latest confirmed case before it can seed further spread in southeastern Minnesota. Britannica Editors Last updated Sep. 15, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Quick Summary Table of Contents Table of Contents Quick Summary Ask Anything Top Questions What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, a hallmark symptom of which is a blotchy rash. It is most common in children and can be prevented through vaccination. What happens if you get measles? If you get measles, you are likely to develop a high fever, cough, and runny nose and have red, watery eyes. These symptoms are followed by a characteristic rash that spreads from the face downward. Symptoms appear 7–14 days after exposure and can lead to severe complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain inflammation), diarrhea, or death, particularly in people who are unvaccinated. Can you get measles if you had a vaccine? It is possible, though rare, to get measles even after being vaccinated. Such breakthrough infections occur because the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, is about 97 percent effective after two doses. However, vaccinated individuals who become infected usually experience a milder illness and are less likely to spread it to others, providing crucial protection for vulnerable populations, including the very young and the elderly. Why is measles coming back? Measles is resurging primarily due to declining vaccination rates, which have dropped below the 95 percent threshold required for herd immunity. Increased vaccine hesitancy and interruptions in routine immunization schedules, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, have been major contributing factors to this decline. Because the measles virus is highly contagious, it spreads easily and quickly through under-vaccinated communities. What is the recommended treatment for measles? No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. What are complications of measles? Measles complications are frequent and include superimposed bacterial ear infection, pneumonia, and lung infection. The virus can also cause hepatitis, appendicitis, and gangrene of the extremities. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Can measles affect adults? Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. Is there a vaccine for measles? Measles vaccines are live vaccines that work against measles alone or in combination with other agents, specifically with rubella (MR), mumps and rubella (MMR), or mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV). The vaccines are typically given in two doses, the first before 15 months of age and the second dose later; timing of the dosages varies by country or region. Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Infants are immune up to four or five months of age if the mother has had the disease. Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. The disease can be prevented through immunization with the MMR vaccine. Learn more in this list of vaccine-preventable diseases. Transmission and symptoms MeaslesGiant cell in a patient with measles.(more) Measles is so highly communicable that the slightest contact with an active case may infect a susceptible person. After an incubation period of about 10 days, the patient develops fever, redness and watering of the eyes, profuse nasal discharge, and congestion of the mucous membranes of the nose and throat—symptoms often mistaken for those of a severe cold. This period of invasion lasts for 48 to 96 hours. The fever increases with appearance of a blotchy rash, and the temperature may rise as high as 40 °C (about 105 °F) when the rash reaches its maximum. Twenty-four to 36 hours before the rash develops, there appear in the mucous membranes of the mouth typical maculae, called Koplik spots—bluish white specks surrounded by bright red areas about 1/32 inch (0.75 mm) in diameter. After a day or two the rash becomes a deeper red and gradually fades, the temperature drops rapidly, and the catarrhal symptoms disappear.
