Britannica Quiz A Visit with the Word Doctor: Medical Vocabulary Quiz Treatment and complications No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. Although uncomplicated measles is seldom fatal, infection with the virus has been shown to induce a form of “immune amnesia,” whereby measles virus eliminates as many as half of the antibodies generated against other infectious agents to which an individual was exposed previously. Thus, persons who survive measles infection may become vulnerable once again to a range of other diseases, such as chickenpox and polio. By contrast, individuals vaccinated against measles do not experience a loss of immunity to other infectious agents. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Complications of measles are frequent and include a superimposed bacterial ear infection or pneumonia or a primary measles lung infection. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Measles virus can invade various organ systems and cause hepatitis, appendicitis, and gangrene of the extremities. A large percentage of cases of severe measles are associated with inadequate intake of vitamin A, and there is evidence that treatment with vitamin A may reduce measles complications. On very rare occasions, persistent infection with a mutant measles virus can cause a degenerative central nervous system disease called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), in which there is a gradual onset of progressive behavioral and intellectual deterioration. Motor incoordination and impairment of speech and sight subsequently develop. The final stages of stupor, dementia, blindness, and death occur within six to nine months. There is no treatment for SSPE. Measles vaccine and eradication efforts How We Develop New VaccinesWorried about diphtheria? No? Thank vaccines.(more) See all videos for this article Mortality caused by measles declined steadily in the 20th century as the health of children and infants improved and effective treatment of complications became possible through the use of sulfonamide and antibiotic drugs. The widespread use of measles vaccine, beginning in the late 1960s, raised hopes for the eventual eradication of the disease. In the following decades, however, measles remained a leading cause of childhood mortality worldwide, primarily because attack rates remained high in less-developed countries, where factors such as malnutrition and weak public health infrastructure challenged infant health and the establishment of immunization programs. In the early 21st century, campaigns were initiated to increase vaccination, particularly in less-developed countries. International efforts led to a significant reduction in measles cases and deaths, bringing global elimination of the disease within reach. At the same time, supporting this progress, many wealthier countries, including the United States and some countries in the European Union, had successfully eradicated measles. Explore Britannica Premium! The trusted destination for professionals, college students, and lifelong learners. SUBSCRIBE In the second decade of the 21st century, however, large measles outbreaks continued to occur in countries with low vaccination rates. In late 2019 in Samoa, for instance, a severe outbreak of measles resulted in school closures and government shutdown, followed by a mass vaccination campaign to prevent further spread of the disease. Measles also reemerged in several countries where it previously had been eradicated, a trend attributed to alarming declines in vaccination coverage. Of particular concern was the return of measles in developed countries such as the United States, where the disease had been eliminated by 2000, and the United Kingdom. In these countries, measles reemerged in the form of small outbreaks that were typically concentrated in areas with relatively high proportions of unvaccinated individuals. In early 2025, the death of a child amid a measles outbreak in Texas marked the country’s first death caused by measles in more than a decade. Coincident with the return of measles in more developed countries, however, was a massive surge in the disease in countries with traditionally low vaccination coverage, resulting in large increases in measles cases worldwide. Global incidence was notably high in 2019, with more than 364,800 cases reported between June and July alone that year—far exceeding the number of cases reported worldwide over that time frame for any year since 2006, according to officials with the World Health Organization (WHO). The largest increases occurred in countries in Africa, Europe, and the Western Pacific. By early 2020 the Democratic Republic of the Congo was in the midst of a severe measles epidemic, with more than 6,000 deaths according to WHO. WHO and health officials in regions affected by measles outbreaks increased efforts to bolster vaccination rates to stop the disease from spreading further. Find out from Dr. Tina Tan of Northwestern University why adult vaccination against various types of diseases is importantLearn about the importance of adult vaccination against measles and other diseases.(more) See all videos for this article Measles vaccines are live vaccines that work against measles alone or in combination against other agents, specifically with rubella (MR), mumps and rubella (MMR), or mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV). The vaccines typically are given in two doses. In the United States, for example, the first dose is given at 12 to 15 months of age, and the second dose is recommended at four to six years. In other countries, the vaccine is given first at nine months and the second dose later. The second dose of MMR must be given at least four weeks after the first dose; in adults whose vaccination status is uncertain, the two doses typically are given four weeks apart. The youngest age at which the vaccines can be given is six months, though revaccination (with two doses) is needed later. See MMR vaccine. Similar illnesses Measles must be differentiated from other disorders accompanied by an eruption. In roseola infantum, a disease seen in babies, a measleslike rash appears after the child has had a high temperature for two or three days, but there is no fever at the time of the rash. German measles (rubella) can be superficially differentiated from measles by the shorter course of the disease and mildness of the symptoms. Sometimes the rashes of scarlet fever, serum reactions, and other conditions may, on certain parts of the body, look like measles. Drugs that may produce rashes similar to measles are phenobarbital, diphenylhydantoin, the sulfonamides, phenolphthalein, and penicillin. A vaccine is a suspension of weakened, killed, or fragmented microorganisms or toxins or other biological preparation, such as those consisting of antibodies, lymphocytes, or mRNA, that is administered primarily to prevent disease. How are vaccines made? A vaccine is produced by first generating the antigen—the component that stimulates the immune system to respond. This antigen can take several forms, including an inactivated virus or bacterium, a purified subunit of the pathogen, or a recombinant protein engineered from it. Once the antigen is produced, it is carefully isolated and purified. Additional ingredients are then incorporated to boost its effectiveness and maintain stability during storage. Finally, the vaccine is manufactured on a large scale and packaged for widespread distribution. What is a vaccine delivery system? A vaccine delivery system refers to the method used to package and administer the immune-stimulating component of a vaccine so that it reaches the appropriate tissue in the body. Common examples include liposomes, emulsions, and microparticles. How do vaccines work? A vaccine works by mimicking an infection, prompting the body to generate antibodies against a specific pathogen. Later, if the vaccinated individual is exposed to that pathogen, the immune system recognizes it quickly and mounts a defense, preventing illness. Top Story Officials urge vigilance after measles in Scottsdale store Stephanie Innes Arizona Republic Sep 18, 2026 Sep 18, 2026 Updated 5 hrs ago × Get your morning recap of today's local news and read the full stories here: tucne.ws/morning Prefer us on Google Learn More Facebook Twitter Bluesky WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link PHOENIX — A person with a confirmed case of measles visited a Scottsdale Walgreens earlier in September and county health officials say any members of the public who were there need to watch for symptoms. The warning comes amid a record-setting year for measles cases in Maricopa County. The person with measles in Scottsdale had a travel-related infection of the highly contagious respiratory illness, and marked the county's 28th case of the year, county health officials say. Other details about the new case: Anyone who visited the Walgreens at 11250 E. Via Linda, Scottsdale, between 8 a.m. and 10:25 a.m. on Sept. 8 should watch for measles symptoms through Sept. 29, county health officials say. The 28 measles cases in Arizona's most populated county is significantly elevated over the average of one case per year during the past three decades. Statewide, 123 measles cases had been reported as of Sept. 15. No deaths have been reported. People are also reading... Kennedy Jr. Arizona has one of the lowest levels of kindergarten vaccination coverage in the United States, making schoolchildren in the state more vulnerable to disease outbreaks than other parts of the country. Listen now and subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | RSS Feed | SoundStack | All Of Our Podcasts An ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 17 was up to 731 cases, 141 hospitalizations, and four confirmed deaths, according to Pennsylvania health officials. The most recent death was an 18-year-old who suffered from a rare but known neurological complication of measles called acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, the Mifflin County, Pennsylvania, coroner said in a Sept. 15 statement. Unvaccinated people who are exposed to the measles virus are at extremely high risk. About 90% of unvaccinated people exposed to the virus will become infected, according to federal, state and county public health officials. The disease is preventable with two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which is typically given during childhood. People born before 1957 or those who had measles as children are generally considered immune. An early dose of MMR is recommended for infants ages 6 to 11 months to protect them against the higher potential for exposure. Symptoms of measles typically appear seven to 12 days after exposure but may take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash that is red, raised, and blotchy; high fever (> 101° F); red, watery eyes; cough; and a runny nose. In some situations, certain people exposed to measles may be eligible for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to reduce their risk of becoming ill. This includes some children under 12 months, pregnant women, and individuals with compromised immune systems. Individuals should contact their health care provider for guidance. Young infants are too young for vaccination against flu, measles, and other viruses. They depend on the people around them to reduce their chances of being exposed to these viruses and becoming sick, Maricopa County health officials said in a news release. The same applies for people who are undergoing cancer treatments, who have had organ transplants, and many other conditions. "Lots of medical risk factors are invisible, so you might never know that you’re around people who are at higher risk of hospitalization or complications from these illnesses," said Dr. Nick Staab, chief medical officer for the Maricopa County Department of Public Health. "By taking these simple preventive steps, we can reduce the chances of serious sickness for our friends and neighbors, and we can keep our own families from losing time at school and work due to sickness." Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Pennsylvania officials report fourth measles-associated death in 'surge' of cases 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Madeline Halpert Getty Images A fourth person has died from complications related to measles in Pennsylvania, say state officials, in an outbreak that has infected hundreds of people. An 18-year-old died from acute encephalomyelitis, a rare and severe neurological complication of measles, the Mifflin County Coroner's Office in Pennsylvania said. The Keystone state has seen over 600 cases of measles this year, primarily in Lancaster County. The US eliminated measles in 2000 with the help of vaccines, but it has this year experienced the highest number of deaths from the virus since the 1990s. Last year, three people - including two children - died from a measles outbreak in Texas that spread predominantly among the Mennonite community. The rising number of cases has come as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates. In Pennsylvania, state and local officials have said the 18-year-old and a 40-year-old - both unvaccinated - died from measles-related complications over the past month. Two infants have also died. US children typically do not receive their first MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine until 12 months of age. The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The highly contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia. To achieve herd immunity, around 95% of the population must have the vaccine, say health officials. Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro posted on X on Tuesday: "This disease was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 - yet decades later, we are seeing it surge due to lower vaccination rates." The reporting of the deaths in Pennsylvania has led to tensions between Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about vaccines and has said he would withhold information about the deaths from the top health official in order to protect the families of the deceased. Kennedy has questioned whether the infant deaths were in fact from measles. A 40-year-old woman died in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, on Saturday, with the coroner saying the cause of death was respiratory failure due to measles. Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni said a six-week-old born with a rare genetic condition, Amish lethal microcephaly, died of measles on 18 August. Diamantoni has said another infant who tested positive for measles died soon after birth on 14 August, with the primary cause of death listed as a spleen laceration. Measles infections can cause the spleen to enlarge, raising the risk of rupture. State health officials have said the death was from a measles infection that resulted in a spleen rupture. In a post on X after the first two deaths in the state, Kennedy accused Shapiro of "political grandstanding". The health secretary said the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would only update its information on deaths once reviews were complete. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it had conducted "rigorous investigations" with the coroner's offices to confirm that the latest two deaths were indeed from measles. "These investigations included confirming clinical evidence of a measles infection, a positive laboratory test, and that the death was not due to an unrelated cause," the health department said. In November, a panel is set to decide whether the US will lose its status of having eliminated measles, which Canada lost last year. Kennedy has been criticised by public health experts who argue his remarks and remaking of US vaccine policy has hindered efforts to stop the outbreaks. A vaccine sceptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the MMR vaccine, which has proven safe and effective. The health secretary has said the worsening measles outbreak is a global problem. Speaking before a Senate committee last month, he said: "A lot of nations have lost their elimination status. The whole world had their worst measles year." supplementary_news.content: News Sports Life Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE New York launches measles dashboard as cases rise statewide Casey Pritchard Middletown Times Herald- Record Sept. 16, 2026, 5:07 a.m. ET As of Sept. 12, there have been six confirmed cases in New York City and 51 outside of NYC. All New Yorkers are urged to protect themselves by making sure they are up to date on their measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. There have been a growing number of cases in upstate New York, including cases associated with both local transmission and domestic travel. The New York State Department of Health launched its new Measles Dashboard, allowing the public and healthcare officials to track local risks and raise awareness about rising measles cases in the state. "Under the leadership of Governor Hochul, we are working closely with local health departments and regional partners to track and contain this recent uptick in measles cases," State Health Commissioner Dr. James McDonald said in a statement. "Measles is highly contagious and can cause serious illness and hospitalizations, yet it is effectively prevented with up-to-date measles immunizations. I urge New Yorkers to check their vaccination status and make sure that they and their families are protected. I also ask health providers to be prepared to diagnose and treat any measles they encounter." Measles in NY schools As students return to school this month, New York counties are responding to a rise in measles cases and communicating as needed with districts and parents. A Cornell University study revealed recently that despite the state's high immunization rates in schools, there are pockets of New York that present risks as infection rates continue to rise well above what they were at the end of last summer. ➤ Click here to see what officials in the mid-Hudson Valley are saying about protecting students from the potentially deadly disease. ➤ Click here to see the New York Measles Dashboard NY measles dashboard by county NY measles dashboard by date What does the measles outbreak in 2026 look like in New York As of Sept. 12, there have been six confirmed measles cases in New York City and 51 outside the city, part of a rising trend in global and domestic cases. There have been a growing number of cases in upstate New York, including the first in Chemung County, which the county health department said on Sept. 14 affected an unvaccinated resident. The cases identified in the state are associated with both local transmission and domestic travel. The department is working with county health departments and local partners to closely monitor and investigate all reported cases, and provide the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to any unvaccinated people who request it. Monitoring and investigation activities, such as contact tracing, are ways public health officials work to keep affected communities safe. Anyone who is contacted during these activities is encouraged to be responsive so that important information can be shared to prevent more infections. All New Yorkers are urged to protect themselves by making sure they are up to date on their MMR vaccines and be aware of health advisories when traveling with unvaccinated people, especially young children. Infants 6 to 11 months old can receive an early dose of the MMR vaccine for protection before travel or if they are otherwise at risk of being exposed. What is measles, including symptoms Measles is a highly contagious, serious respiratory disease that causes rashes and fever. In some cases, measles can reduce the immune system's ability to fight other infections like pneumonia. Measles is caused by a virus that is spread by coughing or sneezing into the air. Individuals can catch the disease by breathing in the virus or, less commonly, by touching a contaminated surface, then touching the eyes, nose or mouth. Serious complications of measles include hospitalization, pneumonia, miscarriage, preterm birth, brain swelling, immune amnesia and death. Long-term serious complications can also include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a brain disease resulting from an earlier measles infection that can lead to permanent brain damage years after the initial infection. The department has released a health advisory for healthcare providers on clinical guidance for measles. Measles vaccine available for most residents The department's travel advisory urging New Yorkers to ensure they are fully vaccinated against measles before international travel or travel to an area in the country experiencing an outbreak can be found by visiting .health.ny.gov/press/releases/2025/2025-04-02_tavel_advisory.htm. Healthcare providers should report suspected measles cases to their local health department. Information on how to contact a local health department can be found by visiting health.ny.gov/contact/contact_information. Visit the department's dedicated measles website at health.ny.gov/diseases/communicable/measles for information about measles, current case numbers, immunization data and information for providers. More information about the measles vaccine can be found by visiting cdc.gov/vaccines/by-disease. By Jen Christensen, CNN Sep 16, 2026 Sep 16, 2026 Updated Sep 16, 2026 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email 1 of 2 Measles vaccination is very safe and highly effective, providing lifelong protection for most people. Joe Raedle/Getty Images via CNN Newsource Measles is an extremely contagious virus, but deaths have been rare in the United States due to high rates of vaccination. Centers for Disease Control via CNN Newsource Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save (CNN) — A fourth person with measles has died in Pennsylvania, the state announced Tuesday — marking the first time in decades the United States has recorded so many deaths in a single year. State Department of Health Launches Tool to Help Track Measles Cases A measles dashboard is now available to track local health risks and stay informed about measles in New York. Measles deaths have been extremely rare in the United States because most people are protected by a highly effective vaccine. But as vaccination rates decline nationally and measles cases rise globally, experts say the death toll from measles may continue to grow in the United States this year and beyond. How common are measles deaths in the United States? The last year with at least four measles deaths in the United States was 1992. Until the recent resurgence in cases, the United States went several years without any measles deaths. Last year, there were three measles deaths, and before then, the last measles death was in 2015, when a Washington state woman died. Before then, the United States hadn’t had a measles death since 2003. This year was already the second record-breaking year in a row for measles cases. As of July, the country has recorded more measles cases than in any other year since 1991. Before the vaccine became available in 1963, measles sickened 3 million to 4 million people and led to about 500 deaths every year in the United States. Measles was declared eliminated from the United States in 2000, but recent outbreaks mean that status will be reassessed in November. In a Tuesday Senate hearing, the nominee for deputy secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, Chris Klomp, appeared to acknowledge the US had lost its elimination status, and endorsed measles vaccination strongly as the best way to regain it. “Unquestionably, the MMR [measles, mumps, rubella] vaccine is the single most effective public health tool that we have against measles,” Klomp, a former healthcare executive, told the Senate Finance Committee in the first of two confirmation hearings over two days. “It’s 97% effective after two doses to preventing transmission, and is the single best thing that we can do to eradicate and establish our exemption from measles again.” How common are measles deaths globally? Measles deaths are much more common in low-income countries with weaker health infrastructure than in the United States or similar countries. Globally, an estimated 95,000 people died from measles in 2024, according to the World Health Organization. Ninety-five percent of those deaths were in low-income countries. Measles is considered the most contagious infectious disease known to humans; up to 9 out of 10 unvaccinated people who come in contact with an infected person will catch the virus. Vaccinations have proven highly successful, preventing an estimated 59 million deaths from 2000 to 2024, WHO said. Before widespread vaccination, measles caused an estimated 2.6 million deaths globally each year. Other high-income countries have seen record numbers of measles cases in recent years as well; last year, Canada reported 5,462 measles cases and two deaths. The country lost its elimination status because of sustained transmission for more than a year, a fact HHS nominee Klomp pointed out. Many countries have lost their elimination status, Klomp told Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon and the ranking member of the finance committee. “We’ve seen vaccination rates dropping all over the world, not just the United States,” Klomp said. Nonetheless, Klomp’s unequivocal embrace of the MMR vaccine contrasted with the mixed messaging from his boss, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic who has downplayed the seriousness of measles. Is this number of deaths unexpected? Globally, measles typically kills nearly 3 out of every 1,000 people who get sick; in the United States, it’s about 1 in 1,000, research shows. As of this week, Pennsylvania had counted at least 693 measles cases, 133 hospitalizations and four deaths, according to the Pennsylvania health department. The official tally is likely an undercount. Measles cases are often unreported when people have milder symptoms and don’t see a doctor who would report the case. Pennsylvania’s death toll is “on the high side,” said Johns Hopkins University Professor Dr. William Moss, an epidemiologist who has studied measles for years. Moss believes the higher number of deaths in Pennsylvania “reflects the fact that these infections occurred in individuals, except for the 18-year-old, with underlying risk factors for severe illness and mortality, particularly the two infants.” One infant who died had a ruptured spleen and died shortly after birth. The other infant had Amish microcephaly, a rare and severe genetic disorder that causes a small head and underdeveloped brain and leaves children with little chance of surviving beyond a couple of months, Moss said. The 40-year-old woman who died had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which increased her risk for a severe lung infection from measles. “They’re all tragic cases, all unvaccinated cases, but kind of unique in their underlying risk factors for severe measles,” Moss said. What is acute disseminated encephalomyelitis? The Mifflin County, Pennsylvania, coroner said this week that an 18-year-old with measles died from acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, known as ADEM. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is a severe neurological complication of measles that triggers rapid inflammation and swelling in the brain and spinal cord. It develops in about 1 in 1,000 measles cases. “It’s just a relatively rare, but known complication of measles that can occur in anyone, even otherwise healthy individuals,” Moss said. Could there be something new or worse about the virus circulating now? Neither Moss nor Dr. David Margolius, director of the Cleveland Department of Health, believes the virus has mutated to become more deadly. There may be more deaths because there are more cases and fewer people are getting vaccinated, Margolius said. “So it’s been given a door in, and it’s taken advantage and the virus has spread across many populations across the world,” Margolius said. Are vaccinated people at risk of death from measles? There is no specific treatment for measles, so prevention is the best way to reduce risk of serious illness or death. The measles vaccine is highly effective, providing 97% protection for most people. “It’s not perfect and we have a two-dose vaccine schedule for a reason,” Moss said. “Not everyone responds to the first dose.” The risk of death from measles for vaccinated people is “very low, unless you’re immunosuppressed in some way,” Moss said. Measles, mumps and rubella protection are combined into one vaccine administered when a baby is between 12 to 15 months old. Children get a second dose between ages 4 and 6. For most people, protection provided by the vaccine lasts a lifetime. Who’s most at risk of serious illness from measles? Measles can be serious for anyone at any age, but some groups are more at risk of serious complications, including: Children younger than 5 Adults older than 20 People who are pregnant People with weakened immune systems from conditions such as HIV or leukemia What are some of the long-term risks of measles infection? Measles is well known for its rash, fever and cough, but it can also cause seizures, blindness, deafness and permanent lung damage. Measles can also weaken the central nervous system and immune system, resulting in serious disease or death years later. The measles virus can also essentially wipe out the body’s previous immune memory, making people vulnerable to other dangerous infections, even long after they recover from the initial infection. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, is a rare but fatal central nervous system disease that can develop seven to 10 years after a person is infected and seems to have recovered. Before vaccination was widely available, about 1,000 people developed chronic disability from acute encephalitis caused by measles annually, according to the CDC. supplementary_news.content_title: New measles cases in Ohio spike 327% as outbreak surges
supplementary_news.content: Wayne County is leading the surge in new measles cases amid Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 . The state had 47 new cases in the past week, a 327% increase in the 11 new cases the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. And 34 of those cases are from Wayne County in Northeast Ohio. That's nearly quadruple (a 378% increase) its nine cases the week prior. ODH is reporting 180 cases in 15 counties this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Sept. 17. That's up from 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10; 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3; 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27; 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20; 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13; and 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Tuscarawas County announced its 13th confirmed measles case on Sept. 16. The individual is the first Tuscarawas County measles case identified during the current outbreak who was fully vaccinated against measles. Two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles infection when exposed to the virus. "Although rare, breakthrough measles infections can occur among fully vaccinated individuals, particularly in areas where measles transmission is widespread, as we are currently experiencing in Ohio," said Katie Seward, Tuscarawas County health commissioner. "Fortunately, this individual is experiencing mild symptoms and is recovering at home. We continue to encourage residents to talk with their healthcare provider and make sure they and their families are up to date on recommended vaccinations."The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. "It's unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable," Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. "This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated." Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Sept. 11 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 3,387 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Once-eradicated disease returns: Measles cases hit highest level in 35 years Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: The case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February . The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. At least two people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania, according to USA TODAY . Both were unvaccinated and both were infants, the Lancaster County coroner said, according to CBS News . The measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release , and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data . US measles cases: 3 states battling new outbreaks. What to know Portage County confirmed its first measles case, the county Health District announced Sept. 8 . At the time, no public exposure locations associated with this case had been identified. While Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, the state dashboard shows additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reports some of its cases are likely associated with a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. One of the Tuscarawas cases is from the same event, that county health department reports. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. See the charts: Measles cases reach highest level in 35 years Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years , resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC . In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr . as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A . During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine . President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY . "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates , according to experts . The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization . Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Disease outbreak: Senator Warnock calls for RFK Jr.'s resignation as measles cases spike Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic . Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images Trump administration changes how it counts measles deaths amid Pennsylvania outbreak CDC announces changes to how it reports measles deaths as Pennsylvania continues to confirm more cases The Trump administration has changed the way it counts measles deaths amid an outbreak in Pennsylvania, which on Sunday saw the third apparent measles-related death in the state reported by a local coroner. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is now using data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which is a way to track mortality trends over time, according to a note published to the agency’s website on 4 September. It’s a “puzzling” move, said Debra Houry, a former CDC chief medical officer. “The change doesn’t make any sense,” she added. This system is “not meant to confirm an individual case”; instead, it’s “usually focused on high-quality, long-term mortality trend analysis”, she said. Pennsylvania reports apparent third measles-related death amid outbreak Read more Previously, the CDC used a system called the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), which the agency has described as the supply chain for data from local jurisdictions and states to the federal government. “CDC will report measles deaths if and when the National Center for Health Statistics reports measles as the underlying cause of death,” said Emily Hilliard, a US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) spokesperson. The CDC put an asterisk under its tally of deaths that leads to a note saying the NCHS “does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause”. Officials in Pennsylvania have confirmed two deaths this year, a newborn and a six-week-old infant, associated with measles. And a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson county, Pennsylvania, died on Saturday from probable measles, said Greg Furlong, the county’s coroner. The woman was unvaccinated and she had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with 24/7 oxygen support, both of which made her vulnerable to complications. The woman had not sought medical care for her apparent infection. “They were going to, but obviously got to the point where it turned to the worst and ultimately led to her death,” Furlong said. She had the classic measles rash and other symptoms, and a close contact had recently tested positive for measles. A nasal swab is undergoing testing for measles and results are expected within days. But the death will be classified as probable measles-related because of the epidemiological connection to a confirmed case, Furlong said. The woman would not have died without the measles case, despite her conditions, the coroner said. “None of us know when our last day is here on this Earth,” he said. “But I strongly 100% believe if this wouldn’t have come into her life that she would be alive today,” he said, adding: “Even with her underlying conditions, I believe she’d be alive today.” Maintaining a measles immunization rate of at least 95% is “absolutely” important for protecting people who are vulnerable to infection, Furlong said. That’s especially true for those who can’t be vaccinated, like infants under the age of six months and pregnant people. “We can all learn from this, and hopefully we can encourage more people who aren’t immunized to get immunized,” Furlong said, adding: “People do not want to be a statistic. “Hopefully this is something that more people get tested, more people get immunized. It’s something we thought we had eradicated, and here we are,” he said. “But it’s a shame that had to lead to somebody’s death.” Pennsylvania had 676 confirmed measles cases as of Friday, but Furlong said he believed the official case numbers are an undercount and there are more infections that are not being reported. “I 100% guarantee it,” he said. Furlong made the announcement on Sunday because “it’s informing people of something that we should all be aware of”, he said. Once the Pennsylvania department of health completes its investigation of the death, including the results from the nasal swab, it will notify the CDC of the case. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the HHS secretary, has not commented on the death, posting on X about fitness, Medicaid and Medicare fraud, and screen time. Kennedy previously argued without evidence that the two earlier deaths may not be from measles, and he asked Erica Schwartz, the CDC’s director, not to count the deaths in the official CDC tally, according to reporting by Reuters. The day after the Reuters report was published, the CDC changed its data source on measles deaths. Kennedy also spent nearly two decades at the helm of the Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization, and he has repeatedly spread misinformation about vaccines. “CDC’s recommendation for the MMR vaccine has remained unchanged, and the Secretary has repeatedly said that the MMR vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent measles infection,” Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS) By Leif Greiss | lgreiss@mcall.com | The Morning Call PUBLISHED: September 17, 2026 at 7:00 AM EDT | UPDATED: September 17, 2026 at 7:01 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Cases of measles continue to rise in Pennsylvania, with nearly 117 new cases reported in the last week, but no new cases in the Lehigh Valley. As of Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 731 measles cases since the beginning of the year, with about 141 resulting in hospitalizations. Hospitalizations rose dramatically since last week, up nearly 29%. Four deaths have been reported during the outbreak so far: two in Lancaster County, one in Jefferson County and one in Mifflin County. Though measles is often associated with children, the majority of cases and hospitalizations have been among adults. Adults between 18 and 49 years of age have been most impacted by this year’s measles outbreak, and made up more than 70% of hospitalizations and about 69% of cases. Lancaster County continues to lead the state with 308 cases as of Wednesday. Mifflin has become the second-highest at 83 and has the highest rate per capita for the entire state, with roughly 2 cases per 1,000 people. Cases have been reported in 38 counties, including two in Lehigh County. However, the only counties where there is believed to be active community transmission are Centre, Chester, Clearfield, Indiana, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mifflin, Snyder, Somerset, Union and York counties. There is no active risk of spread in the Lehigh Valley, nor any of the immediate surrounding counties. Measles is a highly contagious respiratory disease caused by a viral infection. The virus spreads when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks, and lingers in the air. Entering a room where someone with measles was two hours prior can lead to contracting the virus. People with measles are infectious up to four days before a rash appears and up to four days afterward. Across the country, there have been at least 3,294 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, with cases reported in all but five states. The most cases have been reported in South Carolina, Pennsylvania and Utah, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The best protection against measles is getting fully vaccinated. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, administered in two doses, boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97% lifetime protection. Less than 1% of measles cases identified in Pennsylvania have been among people who are fully vaccinated. The press release stated the health department is investigating one unvaccinated person who began showing symptoms on Sept. 3. Officials identified “possible public exposure sites” and reached out to known contacts of the infected person. County Public Health Director Pete Buzzetti told WSKG in a phone call that the county would not provide additional details about geographic location, age, gender or possible hospitalization because he said there is “not a lot of information that can be shared without potentially identifying the individual.” “This work is done hand-in-hand with the [New York State Department of Health]. They know all of this information,” commented Buzzetti. He said the county would share more information if this were a case where the person was in a “high traffic area” such as a performance venue or a grocery store, and health officials needed to alert more people. Buzetti said measles is very contagious and airborne and stated there could be more cases given the county’s 75 percent vaccination rate for Measles, Mumps, Rubella (MMR) and the way the virus is “traveling around” in neighboring counties. However, he said any additional cases would not necessarily be related to the one identified case in Chemung County. Since August, several upstate counties have confirmed nearly 20 measles cases combined, including one case in Tioga County, five in Otsego County and 10 in Steuben County. All of the people infected in these counties to date are unvaccinated. There are currently 3,387 measles cases reported nationwide, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health U.S. Measles Tracker. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says that “vaccine coverage of at least [95 percent] with both doses of measles vaccine prevents outbreaks and protects communities.” Buzzetti said “the public is not as into vaccines as they used to be” and he “supports people’s right to make decisions for themselves and their families.” “The vaccine’s available,” said Buzzetti. “It’s available in a lot of places. It’s really the best line of defense. But for those people that don’t believe in that, I respect that.” The Chemung County press release stated the overall risk for measles to the general public is low, especially in fully vaccinated individuals. People who are unvaccinated, pregnant, under 12 months of age or have weakened immune systems are at higher risk and should consult their health care provider. Information about vaccination access and availability through your local public health departments can found on their respective county websites. supplementary_news.content_title: Missouri train ride led to Kansas City-area measles case that’s exposed 250 people so far
supplementary_news.content: Jackson County health officials are still working to trace potential exposures to a single measles case reported Sept. 13. (photo submitted). It was the call Ray Dlugolecki had been dreading. And one he and other public health officials have been expecting. The assistant director at Jackson County Public Health learned on Sunday afternoon about a confirmed case of measles, not just in his agency's jurisdiction, but in one of its own buildings. The previous week, an infected resident of eastern Jackson County had been inside the health department's Lee's Summit facility at 3651 N.E. Ralph Powell Road on two separate occasions. Dlugolecki understood that the highly contagious virus, which has been spreading with increasing success in communities around the country, had finally reached his doorstep. The welcome mat — a countywide vaccination rate too low for herd immunity — seemed to have made the scenario almost inevitable. County officials said the person likely contracted the virus on an Amtrak train traveling from Sedalia to Chicago on Aug. 27. And now, that single case has exposed more than 250 people in Jackson County to measles, a dangerous virus that had been all but eliminated in the United States only a few years ago. That number doesn't include anyone across the state line in Johnson County who could have also been exposed. "If we have pockets of individuals who are unvaccinated or can't receive vaccines," Dlugolecki said, "it gives the virus the opportunity to enter those communities and spread like wildfire." Immediately after learning about the Lee's Summit exposure, a team of six Jackson County Public Health employees came into the office to begin trying to trace the infected person's movements and figure out where they could have been infected. They worked into the night tracking down and notifying anyone who was in the room when the infected person was there or during a window after the person left. The measles virus can linger in the air as long as two hours. So far, the health department has identified 251 people who had been exposed in Jackson County by this one case, including at least 10 who now have to quarantine for 21 days because they were not vaccinated or did not know their vaccination status. And area health officials expect the number of people exposed to grow. The team also traced the infected individual's movements to public spaces in Overland Park, where the Johnson County Department of Health and Environment also opened an investigation. Johnson County Health Director Charlie Hunt said no new cases had been identified by Sept. 16, but that could change, as symptoms can take seven to 14 days to show up. Jackson County Public Health investigators said the local case is directly connected to another recent measles case of a Missouri resident who boarded Amtrak train 318 , the Missouri River Runner, in Sedalia on Aug. 27 and rode to Chicago. Dlugolecki said evidence, including the timing of travel, symptom onset and epidemiologic information available, means the cases are likely linked. According to state officials, two other measles cases have also stemmed from that person on the train — one in another person on board, and one in someone who lived in the same household — bringing the total cases related to the Amtrak exposure to four. To achieve herd immunity for measles, at least 95% of people must be vaccinated. But across the country growing distrust in public health and misinformation about vaccines has caused that number to fall below that threshold. According to most recent data, in 2025 only 89.5% of Missouri kindergartners and 90.26% of Kansas kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella. Recent data show a sharp rise in the number of parents seeking exemptions so their children can attend school without getting required shots. Missouri's exemption rate jumped to 6.3% in the 2025-26 school year from 5.2% a year earlier, while Kansas' jumped to 4.5% from 3.6%. Growing fear stoked by misinformation about the safety of vaccines — including some coming from the White House — is likely partially to blame. And, since the COVID pandemic, public health guidance of almost any kind has been greeted with more skepticism overall. But whatever the cause of declining vaccine coverage, the result is a population potentially ripe for an outbreak, KC-area public health officials said. One infected person walking into a room with unvaccinated people could quickly spiral into a dangerous situation. In fact it is almost certain nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed will get sick. "People have to realize there are constant sparks getting thrown," said Nathan Koffarnus, an epidemiologist with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. "It's just where they land, that's the luck of the draw. ... Now that there are more people walking around unprotected or underprotected, it's a larger issue again." The measles virus spreads through the air when someone who is infected coughs, sneezes or talks. It can also be picked up from a contaminated surface like a countertop or table. Two shots of the MMR vaccine, the recommended dose, are 97% effective, meaning if 100 vaccinated people are exposed, only three might develop the virus. That makes the MMR vaccine one of the most effective out there. For comparison, the influenza vaccine is typically only 30% to 50% effective, in large part because influenza, like the virus that causes COVID, mutates, creating a changing target that is more difficult for a vaccine to hit. So far this year, of the 3,294 people known to have contracted measles in the United States, 95% were not vaccinated . But rarely, people who get an MMR vaccine still get sick. That was what happened in the recent Lee's Summit measles case. Dlugolecki said the person at the center of the case had been vaccinated. Catherine Satterwhite, executive director of the Center for Population Health and Equity at Kansas City University, said breakthrough cases happen with all vaccines. But in the case of measles, they are exceedingly rare. "For somebody to have a breakthrough case, a lot of things have to happen," she said. Rarely, a person's immune system doesn't respond as expected to the vaccine, leading them to have less protection. It is also possible a vaccine could be somehow corrupted, possibly because it wasn't stored at the proper temperature, causing it to provide less protection. But even people who experience one of those extremely rare problems and get a breakthrough case of measles will still benefit from having been vaccinated, Satterwhite said. A breakthrough infection is usually less severe, comes with fewer serious side effects and is less easily passed on to others. Satterwhite also said the Lee's Summit breakthrough case provides a perfect illustration of why widespread vaccination is so important. "We recommend vaccines on the population level to protect the people who either aren't getting the (immune) response that we expect," she said, "or who can't get vaccinated." The few exceptions include infants. The first MMR dose isn't recommended until a child turns 1, and the second is given around 5 years old. Some immunocompromised people also can't receive the vaccine. Health officials hope that incidents like the recent exposure in Missouri cause more people to understand the risks of not getting the shots. Just being exposed, even without symptoms, will require someone who is not vaccinated to quarantine for 21 days. And developing measles can cause serious illness, including pneumonia, encephalitis and, in rare cases, death. An ongoing outbreak in Pennsylvania is linked to four deaths so far. The virus, which was responsible for 500 deaths every year before vaccines became available, was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. But that status, achieved when there was no continuous spread for more than 12 months, is at risk. Beyond the health costs of a measles outbreak, responding to infections costs tax money. The Washington Post reported that investigating a Colorado outbreak involving nine children and one adult earlier this year cost taxpayers half a million dollars. Jackson County Public Health could not yet offer an exact price tag for their recent case, but Dlugolecki said the agency has already dedicated more than 150 staff hours to the response. That includes epidemiology and communicable disease investigators, leadership, communications, nursing and staff temporarily reassigned from other areas of the health department to help identify and contact exposed individuals, verify immunity, provide quarantine guidance and coordinate follow-up, he said. "That redistribution of staff also means other important public health work has had to pause or slow while the response is underway," Dlugolecki said Each exposed person may require multiple calls, vaccination record review, coordination with healthcare providers or employers, symptom monitoring and follow-up over the 21-day monitoring period. "The larger point is that a measles response can become very resource-intensive very quickly, even when it starts with a single case," Dlugolecki said. "Much of that burden comes from the number of people who may have been exposed and the amount of work required to make sure they are identified, informed and appropriately managed." Declining vaccination rates are the biggest reason the country is seeing more measles cases this year — the most in three decades. In some ways, said Koffarnus of the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the vaccine may have been too effective. "Cases have gone down so much over the past few decades that most people can't remember ever knowing anyone that had it," he said. "When you don't see it and you don't hear about it you think, 'Well, that's not something we have here in the United States.' It's tough for people to take that seriously and think, 'Well, yeah, I probably should get the shot.'" A popular meme often circulated among people who oppose the MMR vaccine involves "The Brady Bunch," a 1960s sitcom. In a 1969 episode , the TV family happily navigates a measles outbreak, gleeful about time off school, appearing to experience very little distress. People cite the show as an example of why measles isn't much to worry about, an inaccurate view, health officials said. But the truth is, the virus wasn't much to worry about in recent years when vaccination rates reached 95% or higher. That wasn't because the virus was no big deal — health experts are quick to point out — but because the virus wasn't spreading. Clearly, that reality has changed, said Dlugolecki, something he didn't expect when he began his public health career 13 years ago. He didn't think waiting for the next report of a measles exposure would be part of his regular workload. "I was shocked to see it come back as it has over the last couple of years," he said. "I didn't expect to see massive outbreaks in dozens of states with deaths being reported." Photograph: Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images Pennsylvania asks CDC for emergency help as measles outbreak spreads State reportedly asks for emergency assistance as state Democratic governor spars with US health secretary Pennsylvania is seeking emergency assistance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as a major measles outbreak spreads across the state. The state warned the request could be withdrawn unless the federal agency publicly recognizes four measles-associated deaths reported by the state. The Pennsylvania department of health has begun the process of requesting CDC emergency support known as an Epi-Aid, according to a letter reviewed by the Guardian. The letter was first reported by Reuters on Thursday. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s secretary of health, outlined the condition in a letter sent on Wednesday to the CDC director, Erica Schwartz. “The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognize the deaths undermines our response,” Bogen wrote. “For this reason, if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the department will respectfully rescind our request for a CDC Epi-Aid.” With US measles deaths on the rise, local officials are stepping in where RFK Jr won’t Read more The development comes amid an ongoing dispute involving Josh Shapiro, the state’s Democratic governor, and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, over the state’s handling of the outbreak and how measles-related deaths are being counted. Kennedy has questioned whether deaths linked to the measles outbreaks since he took office were caused by the virus or by another condition. He also instructed the CDC not to include Pennsylvania’s reported fatalities in the national measles death count last month, a move health experts called “highly unusual” and warned it could lead the public to underestimate the dangers of measles. Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing Pennsylvania’s outbreak and failing to seek out federal assistance. The state’s latest move marks a shift from its earlier position. Pennsylvania health officials had previously resisted CDC assistance, saying they were capable of managing the outbreak without federal help. Since then, the situation has worsened. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania health department announced that 731 measles cases have been confirmed in 38 counties across the state so far this year. Four people have died in the state from measles-related illness as of Tuesday. The CDC did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion The outbreak is among the largest and deadliest in the country and comes as the US experiences its most severe measles resurgence in more than three decades, driven by increasing vaccine hesitancy. This month, it was revealed that the Trump administration changed the way it counts measles deaths amid the outbreak in Pennsylvania. The CDC is now using data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which is a way to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made. On Wednesday, Bill Cassidy, a Republican chair of the Senate health committee, blamed the Trump administration’s vaccine-skeptical approach for the ‌recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania. Email Newsletters Social Media Feedback Contact Us Email Newsletters Social Media Feedback Measles spreads as state begins new vaccination effort; new research shows a way to target efforts WRVO | By Dave Bullard Published September 17, 2026 at 5:15 AM EDT Facebook Bluesky Threads Flipboard LinkedIn Email Print Listen • 5:19 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Measles cases have been slowly rising in New York this year. As of September 12, 2026, there have been 51 confirmed cases of measles. Measles is continuing its slow march across New York state, with the number of confirmed cases through Sept. 12 rising slightly above the total for all of 2025. At least 51 cases of the potentially fatal illness have been reported to the New York State Department of Health, as shown on its new Measles Dashboard. The state is rolling out a new effort to convince people to get vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella, attempting to counter the effects of an anti-vaccination movement that has the support of the Trump administration. A new public service announcement for the general public and a briefing for medical providers aim to raise the statewide vaccination rate. “Sometimes, it's that people really just aren't aware where the vaccine is, or even that it's something you need to do,” said Dr. James McDonald, the state health commissioner. “Sometimes, it's because people really just don't want to get the vaccine.” McDonald calls the vaccination issue a “kitchen table issue” that can be improved through face-to-face discussion. He noted that vaccination rates tend to be lower in more rural areas, where people may lack convenient access to a vaccination site. A study, heavily criticized for its methods, reported a link between the MMR vaccine and autism. No subsequent study confirmed those claims, and even the Trump administration’s Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states on its website: “The vaccine has an excellent safety record. Hundreds of millions of children have safely received the vaccine worldwide.” All children in New York are required to have the MMR vaccine in order to begin public, private or parochial school. The only exception allowed is if a physician certifies that the vaccine will harm the child. The state repealed a provision allowing people to opt out of vaccination on religious grounds. As a result, childhood vaccination rates tend to be very high across the state and have slowly been rising since the COVID-19 pandemic. Adult vaccination rates are lower for several reasons, including the prior ability to claim a religious reason for not being vaccinated and adults moving into New York who are not vaccinated. Most of the cases of measles reported in the state involve adults. NYS Department of Health / Website screenshot Vaccination rates by county for children up to age 2. NYS Health Department data Vaccination rates for all children age 5 and under in New York are rising slowly, according to the state Health Department. Pennsylvania, which maintains a religious exemption from vaccination, is in the midst of a severe outbreak. Nearly 700 cases have been reported in the last six months, with four deaths, and new cases are running at about 100 per week. The two counties with the most measles cases in New York sit along the Pennsylvania border. Measles is among the most contagious diseases. Nine of 10 unvaccinated people exposed to an infected person will get measles, research shows. For that reason, outbreaks tend to start in localized clusters. Measles was declared eliminated in 2000 but has come roaring back as vaccination rates have fallen. A new study may show health officials a way to prevent outbreaks from starting. Cornell University Professor Ana Bento and Siyu Chen, a postdoctoral research associate, surveyed more than 5,000 schools in 45 states for their vaccination rates. They found that the countywide rates of vaccination often reported publicly hid the potential for an outbreak to start in one school. Their research was published in the journal Nature Medicine. “Most counties in the country, even in the New York state area, seemed to be fairly safe,” Bento said. “But as you start kind of looking under the hood and looking at the school district and school level, we started noticing that many schools and many school districts were much lower in vaccine coverage.” Lower vaccination rates meant that a single case of measles would lead to a general outbreak, instead of an outbreak fizzling out in places with vaccine coverage at 95% or higher. Bento said the research shows health officials a way to predict where outbreaks could occur up to several years in advance, allowing them to more precisely target their efforts. “So it might be that your decision to perhaps campaign for increased vaccination might not be one-measure-fits-all,” she said. “But really thinking about some areas within the county that might require a little bit more targeting potentially to make sure that areas are well covered.” The state Health Department does collect and publish school-level vaccination data. Bento’s research suggests that those numbers could be a starting point for efforts to prevent measles outbreaks. report on sexual violence, and Russia’s new missile tactics Pennsylvania Confirms Fourth Measles Death as US Outbreaks Grow Wednesday, 16 September 2026, 14:07 Measles is highly contagious, but fatalities have been uncommon in the United States because vaccination rates are high. Centers for Disease Control A disease once considered eliminated is exposing gaps in vaccination coverage, with vulnerable patients facing the most serious consequences. Pennsylvania has confirmed its fourth measles death. State officials announced it on Tuesday. For the first time in many years, the United States has recorded at least four fatal measles cases in a single year. As reported by CNN For a long time, measles deaths in the United States were extremely rare thanks to high vaccination rates. However, declining vaccination coverage and the spread of measles in various countries are creating conditions for further increases in infections and deaths. The last time at least four people died from measles in the United States was in 1992. Before the current outbreak, the country had gone several years without recording any deaths from the infection. Three people died the previous year, while the last fatal case before that occurred in Washington state in 2015. Earlier, a measles death in the United States was recorded in 2003. Four deaths and hundreds of cases in Pennsylvania This year became the second consecutive record-breaking year for measles cases. As of July, the United States had recorded more cases than in any year since 1991. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, the state had recorded the following this week: at least 693 measles cases; 133 hospitalizations; four deaths. The actual number of patients may be higher. People with mild symptoms do not always seek medical care, so such cases may not be included in official statistics. The measles elimination status that the United States officially achieved in 2000 is to be reviewed in November because of new outbreaks of the infection. William Moss, a professor at Johns Hopkins University, considers the number of deaths in Pennsylvania relatively high. He noted that nearly all of the deceased, except for the 18-year-old patient, had factors that increased their risk of severe disease. All of these cases are tragic. None of the people who died were vaccinated, but at the same time, they had specific underlying risk factors for severe measles. – William Moss Two infants were among those who died. One child suffered a ruptured spleen and died shortly after birth. The other had Amish microcephaly, a rare and severe genetic disorder that causes an abnormally small head and underdevelopment of the brain. The 40-year-old woman had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. This condition increased her risk of severe lung infection. According to the Mifflin County coroner, the 18-year-old patient died from acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a rare complication of measles that causes rapid inflammation and swelling of the brain and spinal cord. This complication occurs in approximately one in 1,000 measles cases. Why deaths are increasing William Moss and Cleveland Department of Health Director David Margolius do not believe that the virus has become more dangerous. In their view, the main reasons for the increase in deaths are the growing number of infections and declining vaccination rates. The virus was essentially given an open door, and it took advantage of that by spreading among many groups of people around the world. – David Margolius Before the vaccine was introduced in 1963, measles affected 3 to 4 million people in the United States every year and caused approximately 500 deaths. Worldwide, before mass vaccination began, the disease claimed around 2.6 million lives annually. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 95,000 people died from measles in 2024. About 95% of these deaths occurred in low-income countries with weaker healthcare systems. Measles is one of the most contagious infections. Up to nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who come into contact with an infected person may contract the disease. According to the World Health Organization, vaccination prevented approximately 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024. Who faces the greatest risk of severe complications Worldwide, measles kills nearly three out of every 1,000 infected people on average. In the United States, the rate is approximately one death per 1,000 cases. There is no specific treatment for measles. The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine provides about 97% protection for most people. It is administered in two doses: the first at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at 4 to 6 years. For most vaccinated people, protection lasts a lifetime. The following groups face the greatest risk of severe complications: children under 5; adults over 20; pregnant women; people with weakened immune systems, including those with HIV or leukemia. Measles can cause more than just a rash, fever, and cough. Possible consequences include seizures, blindness, deafness, and permanent lung damage. The virus can also damage the central nervous and immune systems. One rare, fatal complication is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. It can develop 7 to 10 years after infection, even if a person believed they had fully recovered. Thus, measles deaths in the United States remain unusual, but their number is increasing amid new outbreaks and declining vaccination rates. More interesting materials: A Pennsylvania measles outbreak has been linked to a third death, with 676 reported cases and a growing dispute over vaccination and federal assistance. A six-week-old Pennsylvania girl with measles and lethal Amish microcephaly has died as the state faces a growing outbreak and two reported measles-linked deaths. A child in Los Angeles County died from a rare measles complication, SSPE, highlighting the critical importance of vaccination amid rising measles cases in the US. Amazon launches Alexa+ in India with Hindi and English support Wednesday, 16 September 2026, 14:04 The upgraded assistant is built for everyday bilingual conversations, but its subscription model will differ sharply between Prime and other users. Amazon has launched its Alexa+ conversational assistant in India with support for Hindi and English. The updated service can sustain longer conversations, remember the context of an exchange, and handle complex, multi-step tasks. As informed by Techcrunch Alexa+ is currently available to all users in India through an early access program. Once testing is complete, the service will be offered at no additional cost to Prime subscribers. For other customers, the monthly subscription will cost 2,000 Indian rupees, or approximately $20.85. What Alexa+ can do in India The updated assistant has a more natural and expressive voice. Alexa+ can handle multi-step requests – for example, ordering products through Amazon’s quick-commerce service Amazon Now and controlling smart home devices. During a conversation, users can switch seamlessly between English and Hindi. The assistant also works with popular Indian platforms and services, including: the Swiggy food delivery service; Zomato’s District ticket-booking platform; the Tripadvisor and MakeMyTrip travel platforms; the EazyDiner restaurant table-booking app. For listening to music, Alexa+ supports Amazon Music and JioSaavn. In June, users were invited to test a Hindi-speaking version of the assistant. The company later began testing an English-language version. Amazon introduced Alexa in India in 2017 with support for English, and added Hindi two years later. India has more than 600 million Hindi speakers, so the company views the Indian market as an important avenue for expanding the presence of its smart devices and digital services. According to Amazon, sales of smart home devices in India increased by 20% over the year. However, the company did not disclose the absolute number of devices sold. Amazon first unveiled the generative version of Alexa+ in 2025. In 2026, the service became available to all users in the United States. That same year, the assistant launched in the United Kingdom, Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Italy, and Germany, with adaptations for local languages and cultural nuances. The launch of Alexa+ in India expands the assistant’s international presence and makes it more accessible to a multilingual audience that uses Hindi and English in the same conversation every day. More interesting materials: Amazon will make Alexa+ free for compatible Fire TV devices in the United States, including for users without a Prime subscription. Amazon invites Indian users to beta test Alexa+ in Hindi, collecting feedback on language handling and local nuances as it prepares deeper localization; sign-ups reportedly close June 22.
