Photograph: Annie Rice/AP Pennsylvania reports apparent third measles-related death amid outbreak Jefferson county coroner says 40-year-old woman died on Saturday, while two infants died with disease in August A coroner in Pennsylvania announced the death of a 40-year-old woman associated with the state’s ongoing measles outbreak. The death appears to mark the third in the US state’s ongoing outbreak. Two previous deaths in the state were in infant children. In one case, the infant was born with a genetic defect that made her vulnerable to infection. The second infant child was infected with measles, and died of a ruptured spleen. The woman died on Saturday, according to reporting by WTAE in Pittsburgh. “Many people associate measles with a childhood illness, but it can lead to severe complications in individuals of any age,” Jason Stiver, the Jefferson county chief deputy coroner and public relations officer, told WTAE. Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, and hospitalizes one in every five unvaccinated people it infects. Between one and three children in every 1,000 die from measles-related respiratory and neurologic complications. Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania Read more “Measles is highly contagious and can result in serious respiratory illness, hospitalization, and in rare cases like this, death. We encourage residents to stay informed, follow guidance from public health officials, and take appropriate steps to protect themselves and their families,” Stiver said. “While cases of severe illness remain uncommon, this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly,” he said. The coroner’s office is reportedly working with Pennsylvania state health officials on the case. The health department released its latest measles update on Friday, which did not reflect the death. As of last week, the state had nearly 700 cases of measles across 37 counties. The outbreak is heavily concentrated in Lancaster and Mifflin counties, where there are large farming communities. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recently released data showing a steady decline in kindergarten vaccination rates, including among the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Experts blamed the decline on the success of the vaccine itself – few people remember a time when children regularly died of measles – and confusion caused by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary and a longtime vaccine skeptic who has repeatedly linked vaccines to autism without evidence. Most recently, Kennedy reportedly asked the CDC to exclude Pennsylvania’s two measles deaths from its tally, and later acknowledged in a social media post that the CDC “waited for the evidence”. Pennsylvania state health officials have counted both deaths as measles-associated. “The Lancaster County Coroner has now publicly stated that measles caused only the second infant’s death and has also publicly stated that the infant had Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic condition in which infants typically live only about six months, received palliative care continuously from birth, and died at approximately two months of age,” said Kennedy. “The Coroner continues to state publicly that the first infant died from a lacerated spleen, not measles.” Explore more on these topics Pennsylvania MMR Health Robert F Kennedy Jr Trump administration US politics Infectious diseases news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Live Trump and leaders of Denmark and Greenland announce plan to sign Arctic security pact next week – live This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myselfJonathan Freedland The week around the world in 20 pictures Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy murder trial speaks out Most viewed Most viewed

By Abby Kousouris Published: Sep. 16, 2026 at 9:55 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google ATLANTA, Ga. — One month after taking over an embattled CDC, new Director Dr. Erica Schwartz sat down with our Georgia Capitol reporter, Abby Kousouris, for a Gray exclusive interview. Schwartz spoke about rising outbreaks and staffing cuts. The one-on-one interview took place at the Georgia Aquarium, where Schwartz addressed a crowded ballroom of health executives. Schwartz called the sit-down an essential handshake with a skeptical public. She said she is determined to rebuild trust and steady an anxious workforce before the next crisis. Addressing the measles surge Inside the ballroom, hundreds of top health executives waited to hear from Schwartz, who spent her first month as CDC director out of sight. Before taking the stage, Schwartz spoke with Kousouris for nearly 40 minutes. The nation is battling its worst measles surge in 30 years, and kindergarten vaccination rates have slipped below the 95% threshold considered safe. W. Nile worries rise after death, positive tests here and elsewhere Health officials say West Nile virus has been detected in mosquitoes at Fort Gordon. “Measles is the most contagious disease,” Schwartz said. “You could have pneumonia. You could get subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which is nearly fatal, and you could die. The MMR vaccine is safe and effective.” Contrasting messages Schwartz’s message differs from that of her boss, Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has called measles a mild illness and questioned the vaccine. Asked whether she is prepared to push back when evidence contradicts Kennedy, Schwartz said, “In the uniformed services, we have something called ‘But sir, but ma’am,’ which means you can disagree. Secretary Kennedy and I have worked together for five weeks now, and I can tell you there have been a few ‘But sirs’ behind closed doors.” AU to launch first public health undergraduate degree program Augusta University is preparing to offer its first undergraduate degree program in public health after approval by regents. The CDC has faced criticism for removing certified Pennsylvania measles deaths from its dashboard after Kennedy called them “fabricated.” Schwartz said the CDC has never had an official definition for a measles death but is working to create one. “If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have COVID, often that was called a COVID-related death,” Schwartz said. “But definitions matter.” Staff morale amid layoffs A year after Officer David Rose was shot and killed near the CDC campus by an accused anti-vaccine gunman, deep federal layoffs have left remaining scientists on edge. Schwartz said she experienced that tension firsthand at her first all-hands meeting. “A young man was asking a question, and he was so nervous — and actually, it wasn’t even nervousness,” Schwartz said. “He was afraid to ask the question. And so, you could tell that there was just a lack of psychological safety.” Schwartz said she is focused on winning over the public one conversation at a time. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. Airlifted to Rochester September 18, 2026 Shares Share Email Share With Measles cases continuing to rise, with one case reported in Cortland County, the New York State Department of Health has officially launched a Measles dashboard. The Department of Health (DOH) urges residents to ensure they are current with recommended immunizations, including Measles-Mumps-Rubella (MMR). The dashboard will allow both the general public and healthcare officials to track local health risks and raise awareness about measles. “We are working closely with local health departments and regional partners to track and contain this recent uptick in measles cases,” State Health Commissioner Dr. James McDonald said. “Measles is highly contagious and can cause serious illness and hospitalizations, yet it is effectively prevented with up-to-date measles immunizations. I urge New Yorkers to check their vaccination status and make sure that they and their families are protected. I also ask health providers to be prepared to diagnose and treat any measles they encounter.” The DOH says 57 confirmed cases have been reported throughout the state, including 51 outside the New York City area. An increase in cases have been reported for Upstate New York, according to the DOH. The DOH says they are working with county health departments and local partners to closely monitor and investigate all reported cases, and to provide measles, mumps and rubella vaccines to any unvaccinated individuals. Measles is a highly contagious, serious respiratory disease that causes rash and fever. In some cases, measles can reduce the immune system’s ability to fight other infections like pneumonia. Measles is caused by a virus that is spread by coughing or sneezing into the air. Individuals can catch the disease by breathing in the virus or, less commonly, by touching a contaminated surface, then touching the eyes, nose, or mouth. The DOH says serious complications of measles include hospitalization, pneumonia, miscarriage, preterm birth, brain swelling, immune amnesia and death. Long-term serious complications can also include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a brain disease resulting from an earlier measles infection that can lead to permanent brain damage years after the initial infection. Individuals should check their vaccination status. Anyone who is unsure of their vaccination status should contact a healthcare provider or local health department. Doctor shares tips amid confirmed Measles case in Maryland WBAL US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 4:35 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 8:09 PM EDT Sep 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Julian Nazario Digital Content Producer Maryland warns of possible measles exposure in Ocean City during Labor Day weekend Updated: 8:09 PM EDT Sep 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Julian Nazario Digital Content Producer BALTIMORE — The Maryland Department of Health is alerting of a possible measles exposure in Ocean City after a person who was visiting during the Labor Day weekend from another state tested positive for measles. Video above: Doctor shares tips amid confirmed measles case in Maryland Advertisement The Department of Health said the anyone who visited the following locations may have been exposed: Casablanca Oceanside Inn from 4 p.m. on Sept. 3 through noon on Sept. 6 Buona Vita Pizzeria on Sept. 3, from 5 - 8 p.m. Bonfire Restaurant on Sept. 5, from 4:30 - 8 p.m Last month, the state declared an outbreak of measles in Carroll, Cecil and St. Mary's counties, as well as identified 14 new confirmed cases in unvaccinated Maryland residents. No public exposures have been identified in these cases. As of Sept. 16, Maryland has confirmed 40 cases of measles. Think you may have been exposed? Here's what to do It can take up to three weeks for symptoms to appear. If someone is not protected from measles, there is a 90% chance they will become infected if they are exposed to it, MDH said. | MDH LINK : Measles fact sheet Were you vaccinated for measles? If you have received two doses of a measles-containing vaccine , or were born before 1957, you are generally considered protected. Check your immunization status securely online via My Immunization Record (MyIR). MDH recommends all eligible people get fully vaccinated against measles. The measles vaccine is routinely recommended at 12-15 months of age for the first dose and the second dose at 4-6 years old. Sometimes a dose is given as early as six to 12 months if there is travel planned to an area that has ongoing measles transmission. Monitor for early symptoms : People, especially those not fully vaccinated or otherwise immune to measles, who were at any of these locations during the possible exposure times should monitor themselves for any early symptoms of measles for 21 days after the potential exposure. Not fully vaccinated or otherwise immune? If you are not fully vaccinated or otherwise immune to measles (i.e., you already had measles) and you might have been exposed, call your health care provider or your local health department to discuss the best next steps for you. If your exposure occurred on or after April 14, 2026, you may qualify for post-exposure treatments. What are the symptoms of measles? Early symptoms of measles are a fever of more than 101 degrees Fahrenheit; runny nose; cough; and red, watery eyes. Usually, one to four days after the early symptoms, a red rash appears on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. Symptoms typically develop 10 to 14 days after exposure but can develop as soon as seven days and as long as 21 days after exposure. A person with measles is contagious, beginning four days before the rash appears until four days after the rash begins. Call your health care provider : Exposed individuals who develop a fever or other symptoms of measles should not go to child care, school, work, or out in public, and should contact their health care provider. They should call their health care provider before going to a waiting room or emergency department so that the facility can take measures to prevent measles from spreading to others. Is measles contagious? Health officials describe measles as a highly contagious disease that is spread easily through the air when an infectious person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area. The disease is also spread by direct contact and after touching infected surfaces. Published September 14, 2026 • Updated on September 14, 2026 at 9:38 am Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER 0:00 Pause 0:01 / 0:29 Unmute Subtitles EnglishNoneSettings ShareToggle Fullscreen the football game and described the incident at the cross NBC Universal, Inc. A second measles case has been confirmed in Kane County, with a vaccinated individual being diagnosed after contact with the initial patient Health officials in the Chicago area are warning about a growing measles outbreak in southwestern Wisconsin, a popular destination for northern Illinois travelers, where more than 160 cases have been reported. The warning came after Chicago officials warned of a possible exposure at Union Station, and Kane County recorded its second measles case of the year. The most recent case, involving a vaccinated person, was linked to an initial case reported in August. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE "The first measles case in Kane County this year demonstrated how quickly measles can create a significant public health response," health officials said. "That individual had up to 1,600 potential exposures, requiring the Kane County Health Department to identify and notify people who may have been exposed and provide guidance to help prevent further spread." "Vaccination greatly reduces the risk of getting measles, but breakthrough infections can occur," Kane County health officials said. "Even when a vaccinated person develops measles, vaccination generally provides protection against severe illness and complications." Anyone with symptoms of measles -- which include high fever, cough, runny nose, watery eyes and a rash -- is advised to not go to an emergency room or doctor's office without calling ahead. "Measles is highly contagious, and arriving without advance notice could expose other patients and healthcare workers," officials said in the alert. Kane County also warned that cases were spreading just over the border in Wisconsin, with more than 163 measles cases recorded so far as of Sept. 10. Of those, 162 cases were in people who hadn't been vaccinated. Additional probable measles cases were also reported in southwestern Wisconsin, including Grant, Iowa and Lafayette counties, the Kane County Health Department said. Public health officials in Wisconsin said measles is continuing to spread locally in the area. "Southwestern Wisconsin is a popular destination for visitors from northern Illinois, including during the Labor Day holiday weekend," Kane County said. "People who traveled to the area recently may have spent time in communities where measles is currently spreading. KCHD encourages residents who traveled to southwestern Wisconsin to be aware of the ongoing outbreak and to monitor for symptoms of measles, particularly if they are not vaccinated or are unsure of their vaccination status." Anyone who isn't sure if they received the recommended vaccine doses is encouraged to check their immunization records, contact their doctor or visit the Illinois Department of Public Health vaccination portal here. supplementary_news.content: ST. LOUIS, Mo. — The St. Louis County Department of Public Health (DPH) said it has detected the first measles case in a county resident in twenty years. Officials said the individual is fully vaccinated and boarded a train for Chicago from Sedalia, Mo., on Aug. 27. DPH is working closely with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services (DHSS) and other public health partners to investigate the case, identify individuals who may have been exposed and provide them with guidance about quarantine or isolation requirements. “Measles is one of the most contagious diseases we see, which is why identifying potential exposures quickly is so important as is abiding by isolation and quarantine requests by the health department” said Director of the Saint Louis County Department of Public Health Dr. Kanika Cunningham in a press release . “Our public health team is actively investigating this case and working with our state and local partners to identify anyone who may have been exposed. We encourage residents not to panic, but to be aware of the symptoms, review their vaccination status and contact their healthcare provider if they develop symptoms consistent with measles." Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The virus can remain in the environment for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. “A vaccine prevents you from becoming ill and passing a potentially deadly virus to a close family member, friend, or neighbor,” said County Executive Dr. Sam Page in a press release. “We encourage families to make sure their children are up to date on their recommended vaccinations and for adults to talk with their doctors if they have questions about their immunity.” Measles symptoms typically begin seven to 14 days after an exposure but can appear as late as 21 days after exposure. Early symptoms commonly include: - High fever - Cough - Runny nose - Red or watery eyes Anyone who believes they may have been exposed to measles should contact their healthcare provider promptly for guidance, particularly if they are not vaccinated or are unsure of their vaccination status. The best way to protect against measles is vaccination with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Two doses of MMR vaccine are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles

supplementary_news.content: 0 seconds of 2 minutes, 20 seconds Volume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard Shortcuts Play/Pause SPACE Increase Volume ↑ Decrease Volume ↓ Seek Forward → Seek Backward ← Captions On/Off c Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreen f Mute/Unmute m Decrease Caption Size - Increase Caption Size + or = Seek % 0-9 Live 00:01 02:19 02:20 Pennsylvania reports fourth death linked to measles 02:20 Get more news on Sept. 15, 2026, 6:41 PM UTC / Updated Sept. 15, 2026, 10:39 PM UTC By Aria Bendix and Erika Edwards A fourth death has been linked to measles in Pennsylvania, the state Health Department said Tuesday. All four deaths have been reported in the last month as Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to grow. They are the first deaths associated with measles in the state in 35 years. In all of last year, the U.S. recorded three measles deaths. The Health Department said in a news release Tuesday that the two people who died most recently were from Jefferson and Mifflin counties. Both were unvaccinated, it said. The Mifflin County coroner said Tuesday that an 18-year-old resident died “due to complications of measles,” specifically a rare and severe neurological condition that causes inflammation in the brain. The Jefferson County resident was a 40-year-old woman with asthma and severe lung disease who died Saturday, the coroner previously reported. The two deaths in Lancaster County were of infants: a newborn who died shortly after birth and a 6-week-old. The county coroner has said he believes measles was only the cause of death for the 6-week-old baby . In the case of the newborn, the coroner said he found evidence of the measles virus in the infant’s lung tissue but considered the cause of death to be an internal hemorrhage and “traumatic rupture” of the spleen. The first dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is typically given at around 1 year, so neither infant had been eligible to receive it. Two doses offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life (the second is given at around age 5). The state Health Department considers a death to be “measles associated” if there is clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive laboratory test and if the death occurred within 30 days of symptoms’ starting. It also takes into account the person’s medical records and whether they were exposed to measles before they died. The department said in a news release that the two latest deaths were linked to measles after rigorous investigations involving the county coroners’ offices. The two infants’ deaths involved similar investigations, the department said. Nearly 700 measles cases have been reported in Pennsylvania this year; 133 people have been hospitalized. State officials have tied the outbreak to falling vaccination rates. Nationwide, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 3,294 measles cases, including 267 hospitalizations, as of Thursday. The CDC has not yet confirmed any of the deaths reported in Pennsylvania, and it says on its website that it does not have any death records from 2026 indicating measles was the underlying cause. Traditionally, the CDC has accepted death reports like Pennsylvania’s from state health departments; the discrepancy is a significant departure from the way the agency has operated in the past. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said Monday that Pennsylvania, unlike other states with measles outbreaks, had not requested the CDC’s assistance. However, the Pennsylvania Health Department said it “maintains a strong working relationship with the professional staff at the CDC.” It also said it submits death records to the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics “daily,” including for the recent measles-associated deaths. Last month, the deaths of the infants in Lancaster County ignited a flurry of misinformation online , as well as political sparring between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Shapiro accused Kennedy of spreading falsehoods about vaccines, while Kennedy suggested that the deaths may have been “fabricated” and that Shapiro was seeking to profit from them politically. Anti-vaccine activists commonly argue that testing positive for measles does not necessarily mean someone died from the virus if a secondary illness or injury was involved. However, doctors say measles is still the underlying cause in many of those cases, since patients would not have died otherwise. The father of the newborn in Lancaster County told NBC News that the baby had been born prematurely and that his mother had measles. Premature birth is a known complication of measles during pregnancy. Measles can also cause the spleen to enlarge, which raises the risk of rupture. The Lancaster County coroner said he did not find evidence that the newborn’s spleen had been enlarged; however, that can be difficult to detect in an autopsy

Pennsylvania has reported four deaths related to measles in 2026. BSIP/UIG via Getty Images Pennsylvania has reported a fourth death related to measles, the latest in a growing outbreak that has also sparked ongoing political clashes. It has been decades since the United States has tallied this number of measles deaths; 1992 was the last time there were four measles deaths in one year. Last year, there were three US deaths from measles – two in Texas and one in New Mexico. The latest death in Pennsylvania was an unvaccinated teen who lived in Mifflin County. Andrea Alcalde, the county coroner, said the 18-year-old died from acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a rare neurological condition that can occur after an infection. Ad Feedback Previously, the state reported two deaths in infants who had measles. Over the weekend, the Jefferson County coroner reported the death of a 40-year-old woman. “My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly-contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said in a statement Tuesday. “We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR vaccine – which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades.” The MMR vaccine is the best way to protect against measles, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says. Two doses provide 97% protection against measles. Approved since 1963, the vaccine is very safe, and side effects are usually mild and go away on their own, the agency says. However, measles cases have begun to surge as vaccination rates decline. Pennsylvania has counted 693 measles cases in 38 counties this so far this year. Nationally, more than 3,200 measles cases have been reported, according to the CDC. Related article Thin-section transmission electron micrograph, TEM, of a single measles virus particle or virion Callista Images/Image Source/Getty Images Adult woman dies of measles complications in growing Pennsylvania outbreak 4 min read Measles typically causes about 1 in 5 people who aren’t vaccinated to be hospitalized, according to the CDC. As many as 1 out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. One of every 1,000 kids with measles will develop encephalitis, or brain swelling. The virus kills 1 to 3 of every 1,000 children who become infected. In a post on X, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, said these measles-related deaths – the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years – are “tragedies.” “Pennsylvania is experiencing the worst measles outbreak in the country,” he wrote. “This disease was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 — yet decades later, we are seeing it surge due to lower vaccination rates.” Deaths spark political clashes The recent deaths led to a war of words over how measles deaths are counted. So far, the CDC has not counted any measles deaths in 2026. CNN previously reported that the CDC was not counting the first two measles-associated deaths reported by Pennsylvania, saying it doesn’t have enough information to determine whether measles caused or contributed to the fatalities. The decision to exclude the deaths from the agency’s weekly update came from the CDC’s new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz. Shapiro said in late August, when the state announced the first two measles-associated deaths, that he’d declined an offer from US Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for federal help. Shapiro then said he’d told the secretary that his “actions and his rhetoric,” including spreading misinformation about vaccines, was harming communities. Kennedy, an outspoken vaccine skeptic, shot back on social media, accusing Shapiro of fearmongering and the “weaponization of infectious disease” for political gain. He suggested the deaths may have been “altogether fabricated” by one of Shapiro’s “hopeful staffers” to support a narrative that measles infection is more dangerous than it actually is. Related article The exterior of the Center for Disease Control and Prevention main campus in Atlanta, on August 27, 2025. Alyssa Pointer/Reuters Trump’s new CDC director ordered delay in counting 2 measles-related deaths 7 min read The two deaths in Lancaster County were in infants, the county coroner there said, but his office disputed whether one of the deaths was caused by measles. A newborn died of a ruptured spleen, which the coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said his forensic pathologist deemed wasn’t caused by the viral illness. A second death, in a six-week-old infant with a serious genetic condition called Amish lethal microcephaly, was caused by measles, Diamantoni told CNN. After the two additional deaths were reported this week, Shapiro again lashed out at Kennedy. “This serious situation continues to be made worse by RFK Jr. playing games with public health and safety. It’s long past time for @SecKennedy to stop stoking vaccine skepticism and misinformation and compromising the serious mission of the nation’s public health agencies,” Shapiro said in a post on X. “It is also deeply concerning to learn that the Secretary personally intervened in an otherwise administrative process to direct the CDC to not report these Pennsylvania deaths, presumably because it doesn’t fit his phony narrative.” In a response posted on X, Kennedy said Shapiro was politicizing the outbreak “instead of implementing a unified public health response. He continues to point the finger at me and the federal government and to malign the Amish while refusing the federal assistance that might help end the outbreak.” Kennedy also said it’s false that he directed the CDC to “suppress” Pennsylvania deaths. He said the agency “will report measles-caused deaths when the National Center for Health Statistics reports measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states.” CNN’s Deidre McPhillips contributed to this report. supplementary_news.content: ‘Countering federal misinformation has fallen disproportionately on doctors and nurses who never expected to be doing that kind of work.’ Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images/Heather Grubola ‘Countering federal misinformation has fallen disproportionately on doctors and nurses who never expected to be doing that kind of work.’ Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images/Heather Grubola With US measles deaths on the rise, local officials are stepping in where RFK Jr won’t As the country’s top public health official spends his time in office undermining science, doctors and advocates mount an urgent campaign for childhood vaccines O n an early September morning, dozens of families stood in line outside a clinic in Yeadon, Pennsylvania. It was “exclusion day”, the deadline by which students without complete immunizations are barred from returning to class. Instead of turning families away, school district leaders partnered with the county health department to vaccinate kids nearby so they could go back to their desks. That day, 42 middle and high school students were vaccinated to protect against tetanus, pertussis and meningitis, among other diseases. “We’ve been doing this for a couple of years now, and it’s really effective,” said Lora Werner, director of the Delaware county health department. The vaccination day is one piece of the county’s back-to-school immunization campaign, as measles cases climbed to 693 in Pennsylvania as of 14 September and this year so far claimed the lives of four residents . The campaign includes a mobile vaccine clinic – a 33ft traveling RV that brings vaccinations to pop-up community events – school district partnerships and vaccination data transparency, all to keep immunization rates from sliding. The push is a local answer to a national problem. The country’s top public health official, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has spent his time in office questioning the efficacy of vaccines and undermining vaccine science, culminating in a recent Trump executive order that seeks to break apart the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shot and shrink the list of vaccines recommended for American children. The administration’s claims about vaccine safety are not just false, but are actively costing lives, advocates said. With federal guidance no longer reliable, the responsibility for reassuring parents and caretakers has shifted downward to governors and state legislatures, state health departments, healthcare advocacy groups and the doctors on the frontlines. Across the country, they’re mounting an urgent campaign to defend childhood vaccines against a wave of misinformation. “Our responsibility is to demonstrate what the science shows and put out a [vaccine] schedule that people can depend upon that is science-based and evidence-based,” said Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “Measles is a canary in the coal mine and we have to now worry about other vaccine-preventable diseases, which is why the local effort at the state level is so critical.” Executive order creates chaos As children got up to date on their immunizations before the start of the school year, Trump signed the “gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations” executive order, calling to reduce the number of universally recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11 and to split the MMR shot into three separate injections, delivered across additional doctor’s visits. The order arrived with no new scientific evidence behind it. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s hospital of Philadelphia, trains doctors to share with their patients that the MMR vaccine has been used safely in the US for about 60 years. Manufacturers have made clear they have no plans to split it into separate formulations, since doing so would offer no safety benefit, he said. Experts have also noted that more doctor’s visits would lead to more opportunities for missed appointments. For many of the doctors and officials fighting the disinformation, the executive order is the latest development in a pattern set by Kennedy since he was confirmed. Offit recalled when Kennedy went on Fox News last year and falsely claimed the measles vaccine causes blindness and death. “Could he be more dangerously irresponsible?” said Offit. “He should have been fired right there, but he wasn’t. And that’s when he knew: I can say whatever I want with impunity.” Robert F Kennedy Jr with Fox News host Laura Ingraham on 13 February 2025. Photograph: Paul Morigi/Getty Images Vaccine misinformation has led to vaccine hesitancy, Racine said. CDC data shows that the number of kindergarteners claiming vaccine exemptions for the 2025-26 school year hit a record high, while vaccination rates for kindergarteners decreased from the year before. Hesitancy is higher in certain rural areas, he said, and states that once had the highest vaccination rates in the country have fallen as they expanded vaccine exemptions . “This is the last thing parents wanted on their back-to-school list, to be confused about the childhood vaccine schedule or to be worried about their child coming home with measles,” said Shaughnessy Naughton, the founder of the non-profit advocacy group 3.14 Action. “It’s why so many doctors and health professionals are now stepping up and fighting back against these dangerous actors” The pushback is state by state, doctor by doctor Because the federal government has abandoned its traditional role as a trusted, science-based source of vaccine guidance, that responsibility has fallen to state lawmakers and health departments, local public health officials and doctors. Following RFK Jr’s appointment as health secretary, some state legislators examined their statutes on vaccines and removed references to the CDC. In January, dozens of states announced that they would reject the CDC’s guidance. Now, 30 states report relying on a source other than the CDC, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians, for information about childhood vaccines. Fifteen states sued the Trump administration earlier this year over its changes to the childhood vaccine schedule and the dismantling of the CDC’s vaccine advisory panel. They’ve also banded together. California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii formed the West Coast Health Alliance, and 15 states - including Connecticut, Maine, New York and Massachusetts – formed the Northeast Public Health Collaborative, two voluntary coalitions to strengthen regional awareness and preparedness on infectious diseases. Racine said that clear and consistent communication and maintaining vaccine access are key in building trust with the public. That’s why states are reassuring practitioners of the standard vaccine schedule, regulating insurance to make sure companies continue to cover vaccines and launching public service announcements to communicate the importance of getting measles vaccines. Elena Parent, a Democratic state senator from Georgia, outside the CDC headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia, on 25 June 2025. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images For example, the Pennsylvania health department says it is ensuring that residents understand the risks of remaining unvaccinated by sharing videos and infographics that explain how contagious the disease is. The response to messaging has been overwhelmingly positive, a spokesperson for the health department said, with more people choosing to vaccinate themselves and their families far more often than not. In August, healthcare providers in the state administered more than 46,000 MMR doses, compared with roughly 31,000 in the same month last year. Hawaii governor Josh Green, a physician who formed the West Coast Health Alliance, said he treats vaccine communication “like a family physician”, sharing granular, local data with the public rather than vaccine mandates. “I believe that people can and should make some decisions based on their belief system,” Green said. “Of course, however, they should also be given the best information possible.” Green’s urgency is shaped by his experience as a volunteer doctor during Samoa’s catastrophic 2019 measles outbreak, which killed 83 people, most of them young children, after a vaccination scare fueled partly by anti-vaccine activists’ visits to the islands. Kennedy, as part of his career as an anti-vaccine activist, visited Samoa in 2019 to study the MMR vaccine months before the outbreak. “We would go into a village, and we’d find families huddled around a child who had just died,” Green recalled. “We would have a funeral service in the bedroom, and then we would have to walk outside and ask: ‘Does anyone want to be vaccinated?’” Green traveled from village to village vaccinating family members. “We saw the same thing over and over again, people dying right in front of us,” he said. Samoa vaccinated nearly 37,000 people in two days, and the outbreak stopped within a week, Green said. He called the parallels to Kennedy’s current rhetoric “the same kind of stuff” he saw before that crisis. “It’s RFK’s playbook,” he said. “He went into a vulnerable community of people that didn’t have a lot of education [...] and he scared people, and they didn’t get vaccinated, and the country got crushed,” Green said. “Now they’re doing the same thing with other rural communities.” Filling the information vacuum Countering federal misinformation has also fallen disproportionately on doctors and nurses who never expected to be doing that kind of work, health officials said. “Doctors are facing a lot – many of them have never seen measles cases before, and now they’re seeing it for the first time in their lives,” said Jeremy Funk, deputy director of the public health project at the non-profit Protect Our Care. He described an “enormous amount of burden” now being placed on pediatricians and state health officials to walk parents through basic vaccine safety information they never previously had to explain. In Pennsylvania, that responsibility has landed heavily on county health departments – some of which face funding challenges or didn’t exist a few years ago. Delaware county was the largest county in the country without a health department until the pandemic, when the community built its own from scratch. “We wanted to make sure we were meeting people where they were,” said city council member Monica Taylor. The Delaware county health department vaccinated 42 students at a clinic in Yeadon, Pennsylvania, on 9 September. Photograph: Heather Grubola Today, that means school partnerships and a mobile health van bring shots directly to parking lots, parks and community events. “It’s really about being out in the community as much as possible and being accessible,” Taylor said. Werner said Delaware county has not seen a surge in outright vaccine refusal, but has seen rising anxiety, including parents asking whether funding for free vaccine programs will survive, or parents confused by shifting federal signals. “We saw more parents concerned that things might not be available,” Werner said, describing a summer awareness campaign the county launched, aimed particularly at reaching Spanish-speaking families. She credited the state health department with holding regular briefings for county officials and continuing to follow “the science”, even as federal recommendations shifted. Pennsylvania also began publishing school-level vaccination data for the first time this year, letting parents and administrators see exactly where local immunization rates stand and where support is needed. “It’s a really hard place for public health right now with so much divisiveness being promoted,” said Werner. “As public health officials, we really want people, from those who are underinsured to those who are undocumented, to keep themselves safe and have good information to make decisions about it. We want to help people hear the information they need to hear.” Explore more on these topics Vaccines and immunisation Building power MMR Infectious diseases Children Robert F Kennedy Jr US politics Health features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Live Trump and leaders of Denmark and Greenland announce plan to sign Arctic security pact next week – live This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself Jonathan Freedland The week around the world in 20 pictures Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy murder trial speaks out

Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images Republican senator blames Trump administration policies for measles deaths in Pennsylvania Health committee chair Bill Cassidy said fatal outbreak of disease is a ‘terrible legacy’ for Trump administration Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the US Senate health committee, blamed the Trump administration’s vaccine-skeptical approach for ‌recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania and challenged Donald Trump’s pick for surgeon general to directly state that vaccines do not cause autism on Wednesday. Cassidy, a Louisiana physician who chairs the panel, said three people in Pennsylvania had died of measles, with a fourth death under review, because ​of misinformation and misguided policies. His remarks come as the US grapples with its worst measles outbreak in over three decades. “To suffer from any disease is awful, but to suffer one which is avoidable, that’s even worse,” Cassidy said, adding that the country needs health leaders “who make decisions based on science, not politics or ideology”. Fourth person dies of measles-associated illness in US Read more The senator said that the outbreak would be “a terrible legacy for this administration”. The committee is currently considering the Trump-picked Chris Klomp for deputy secretary of health and human services, Nicole Saphier for surgeon general and Timothy Westlake to lead the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. Saphier notably avoided mentioning vaccines directly in her opening remarks, instead expressing her Make America Healthy Again bona fides. “I have long believed that we spend too much time and resources treating chronic disease after it takes hold, and not enough time helping Americans reduce their risk before illness begins. And unfortunately, we’re seeing the consequences of that imbalance right now: rising cancer rates in people under 50, cardiovascular disease that remains the number one killer, but also is largely preventable in lots of cases,” Saphier said. Cassidy pushed Saphier about whether she would tell parents concerned about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine that it does not cause autism. “I’m so sensitive to this because I’ve had wriggle room from people sitting there ... who later use that wriggle room to do things which are quite contrary?” Cassidy said, referring to the various promises that Robert F Kennedy Jr made to the top Republican in his confirmation hearing, only for the health secretary to renege on several occasions. “Would you feel comfortable communicating with clarity ... Is the MMR vaccine extremely lethal, as the president said?” Cassidy asked Saphier. The nominee for surgeon general said that she “cannot speak to what the president has said” but went on to say: “I do not believe the MMR vaccine to be lethal. I believe the MMR vaccine is our greatest tool for combating measles.” Saphier, a practising radiologist and Fox News contributor, added: “The best tool we have to combat these infections to save the most lives and to also create population herd immunity is vaccination against the MMR. I appreciate the president is trying to reach vaccine-hesitant people who are wanting more answers or who are concerned that there are too many doses.” skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Cassidy, however, remained unconvinced by the president’s public health strategy. “I’m not sure that you reach people who are vaccine hesitant by feeding into untruths,” he said. Last month, Cassidy denounced Trump’s “crazy, stupid” claims about the safety of the combined MMR vaccine for undermining faith in immunization. Cassidy previously voted to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, despite disagreements over how to combat vaccine skepticism. He said that Kennedy, who has pushed the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism for decades, had promised him that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) “will not remove statements on their website pointing out that vaccines do not cause autism”. After Kennedy became health secretary, however, the Autism and Vaccines page on the CDC website was altered to undermine that scientific consensus. An asterisk was added to the headline “Vaccines do not cause Autism”, which leads to a footnote pointing out that “the root causes of autism” remain unknown. The virus infects the respiratory tract and then spreads around the body. (3D illustration/Shutterstock) Pennsyvlania is seeking emergency assistance from the CDC regarding its measles outbreak but says the U.S. must aknowledge four measles-related deaths. The state's measles outbreak has become the focus of a standoff between U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Gov. Josh Shapiro. The request marks an about-face for the Pennsylvania health department, which had previously resisted CDC aid. Share The Pennsylvania health department said it was requesting emergency support from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as it grapples with one of the country’s largest and most deadly measles outbreaks, according to a document reviewed by Reuters on Thursday. The request comes on condition that the federal agency recognize four measles-associated deaths reported by the state, raising the stakes in a dispute with the Trump administration. The state’s measles outbreak has become the focus of a standoff between U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat. Kennedy has cast doubt on whether deaths reported in U.S. measles outbreaks since he took office were due to the virus or another cause, and instructed the CDC not to include the Pennsylvania fatalities in a national tally. Disease experts say the move represented highly unusual interference by a health secretary in the determination by state health officials and could minimize the risks of measles in the eyes of the public. Kennedy has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak in his state and of failing to request federal help In a letter sent to CDC director Erica Schwartz on Wednesday evening, reviewed by Reuters, Pennsylvania secretary of health Debra Bogen said the state had begun the process to request emergency assistance from the CDC, known as Epi-Aid. “The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognize the deaths undermines our response,” Bogen wrote. “For this reason, if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the Department will respectfully rescind our request for a CDC Epi-Aid.” The request from the state health department comes after it had resisted CDC help, arguing it had the outbreak under control. In a statement, HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison said CDC had not received Pennsylvania’s request through “normal channels,” and that federal outbreak assistance is a separate issue from the way CDC chooses to tabulate fatality data. “CDC will not submit to political blackmail that conditions critical public health assistance,” said Jamison. “CDC will not allow Governor Shapiro to politicize this process. Growing Outbreak Pennsylvania’s outbreak has since ballooned, growing to more than 700 confirmed cases across 37 counties and four measles-associated deaths, according to the state health department. It is the latest state to grapple with the worst U.S. resurgence of measles in more than three decades, fueled by rising vaccine hesitancy, and coincides with President Donald Trump’s return to office in early 2025. Shapiro has criticized Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has promoted policies to reduce U.S. childhood immunization, for amplifying public fears about vaccines without scientific evidence. Kennedy and Schwartz have blamed Shapiro for not accepting their offers of Epi-Aid, a form of short-term CDC assistance during public health emergencies. The agency sends experts to the site of a disease outbreak, typically for one to three weeks, to provide additional support to state and local health departments. When the Pennsylvania health department announced the first two measles-associated fatalities on Aug. 25, the disease had sickened 393 people across 28 counties. Shapiro praised his health department’s efforts to vaccinate more people, and the state health department declined to ask the CDC to send personnel to help on the ground. The Pennsylvania health department, like other state health departments, has CDC career staff who are permanently assigned to assist the agency and have assisted in the outbreak. CDC Epi-Aid would mark an additional form of federal assistance. The disease has since spread and the pace of new infections has accelerated. One of the fatalities announced this week occurred in Mifflin County, which now has the second highest number of cases in the state and is located over 100 miles from the outbreak’s initial epicenter in Lancaster County. At the same time, the pace of measles vaccinations provided by the state appears to be slowing, according to health department data. In August, the health department administered over 3,500 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which provides 97% protection against infection after two doses. For the first half of September, that number dropped to around 1,100 doses. supplementary_news.content_title: New York state launches new measles database
supplementary_news.content: Concerns over the spike in measles cases across the state continue. Pennsylvania reported its fourth measles-related death yesterday. That’s the most deaths from the disease the United States has seen since the 1990s. New York has also caught some of that overflow. On Tuesday, the state Department of Health’s new measles database reported 51 positive cases of measles in New York. Most of them were listed in upstate New York. That’s an increase compared to last year, when upstate confirmed 28 positive cases throughout the entire year. Health officials say there has been an increased number of reports in rural areas. Officials also suggest parents have children vaccinated against measles, especially if you are traveling to any high-risk areas. "Under the leadership of Governor Hochul, we are working closely with local health departments and regional partners to track and contain this recent uptick in measles cases," State Health Commissioner Dr. James McDonald said in a statement. "Measles is highly contagious and can cause serious illness and hospitalizations, yet it is effectively prevented with up-to-date measles immunizations. I urge New Yorkers to check their vaccination status and make sure that they and their families are protected. I also ask health providers to be prepared to diagnose and treat any measles they encounter." There’s new research coming out of Cornell University that looks at vaccine data from 45 states, 13,000 school districts and 50,000 schools. Typically, the state measures vaccination rates by county. However, Assistant Professor of Disease Ecology Ana Bento suggests diving deeper into measurements per school district. “We started gathering data for school-level vaccination in school districts and then starting to compare it with [the] county level. And it became a problem of averages. We started realizing that even though most counties, across the country, not just New York, seem to be protected hubs for thresholds,” Bento explained. “And many districts actually had a much lower vaccine coverage. So we started noticing this patch-like pattern across many states where you would see these very vulnerable areas within a county that were much, much more vulnerable than the county, on average.” Nearly a dozen counties across the state have found positive cases of the measles this summer. Allegany County has six lab-confirmed cases, while its neighbor to the east, Steuben County, has 10 confirmed cases. Seneca County also has nine positive cases, and Otsego County has seven. All positive cases are reported to be unvaccinated individuals. And in all four of these counties, the state Health Department lists as under 80% vaccination rates . Bento says families often travel outside of county lines, and if they’ve contracted the measles, the disease goes with them. “If the reproductive number is two, if I get infected, there's a chance that I will infect you both because we are here, right? If it's 18 or between 15 and 18, which is a case of measles, you can get 18 cases,” she said. Bento says many of the positive cases for measles in New York are unvaccinated children. The state requires dozens of vaccines before children enter kindergarten in order to attend public school. Those include the MMR vaccine, which protects kids against measles, mumps and rubella. In August, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to split the MMR vaccine into separate shots. That’s serving as guidance from the federal government, but Dr. Mahvash Madni, a pediatrician for the American Academy of Pediatrics, says the sequence of vaccines children receive has been thoroughly studied, and the combined MMR vaccine has been recommended for decades. “We're teaching the immune system, with these vaccines, just like we're teaching babies other skills and how to develop and grow,” Madni said. “So this is a better time for that. It's also the safest time because later on they're going to get exposed. And once they're exposed, it's much more difficult to fight these diseases. Madni says vaccine hesitancy is at a 35-year high. “I'm seeing more hesitancy across the board. I think that's the scarier thing, that people who previously weren't too worried about it and got their older children vaccinated are now questioning things for their younger children,” Madni said. “So I can't pinpoint a certain area or belief system community who is going to hesitate. I think the fear is spreading more throughout everyone.” She says there’s a bit of an “out-of-sight, out-of-mind” mindset. “I think people just don't see it so often. Why are we worried about it? There's been, you know, a lot of talk. People are talking and thinking about natural remedies and organic, which is wonderful,” Madni said. “But we can't have that. That idea about, like, ‘Oh, our bodies can fight these diseases if we just, you know, have the proper nutrients because that's fine for the common cold.’ But when it comes to these very deadly and dangerous diseases, that's a whole different story that we do need to think of different and better ways to fight.” While vaccine exemptions apply for certain religions and some medical reasons, health professionals say herd immunity is the goal, and that begins at 95% vaccination rates. “We have to think about all the children,” Madni said. “Not just what you would want for your child or the community. We all feel for children in the whole country. So that's why it's so important to think of everyone, not just your child or your friend's child, but every child. Every child counts.” “You can develop very serious lingering effects post measles, including deafness, for instance. So there are very serious side effects and long-term effects of actually getting the vaccine,” Bento explained. “Thus far, there has never been serious side effects from getting the vaccine, though, so the infection can cause severe side effects. But the vaccine has never been shown to actually cause side effects.” “So even when you're vaccinated, you still have a chance of getting the disease because the vaccines are about 97% effective with two doses,” Madni said. “But there is that small chance of still getting infected. So, there is a risk to everybody. It is a community and a public health issue because we all are combined.” She recommends speaking to your doctor to learn if you’re healthy enough to receive your measles vaccine. Madni adds that these vaccines often last for life, as well. However, some require booster vaccines as children grow up

Advertisement Updated: 5:28 PM EDT Sep 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Russ Reed Maine CDC reports sixth measles case of 2026, warns of potential exposure at MaineGeneral Express Care in Waterville Updated: 5:28 PM EDT Sep 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Russ Reed AUGUSTA, Maine — The Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) is reporting a confirmed case of measles, the state's sixth of the year, and has issued a warning about potential measles exposure at a Waterville facility. The Maine CDC said Wednesday that it confirmed the latest measles case in an unvaccinated adult from Somerset County on Tuesday, Sept. 15. Advertisement State health officials said potential exposure occurred at the MaineGeneral Express Care location at 211 Main St. in Waterville on Saturday, Sept. 12, between 8 a.m. and 11 a.m. The Maine CDC said it is working with the Waterville facility to inform people who were potentially exposed to measles during the aforementioned timeframe. State health officials also said people who were at that facility during that time should take precautions and watch for symptoms until Oct. 3, which is 21 days after Sept. 12. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, and if one person has measles, 90% of the people close to that person who are not immune will become infected. Symptoms of measles include a fever, a cough, a runny nose, a rash that spreads from the head down and red, watery eyes. The Maine CDC said people who develop measles symptoms should contact their healthcare provider for instructions before going to the provider's office or a hospital, as this will help prevent the spread of further infection. Health officials said the measles virus remains alive for up to two hours on surfaces and in the air. Measles can cause severe sickness, including pneumonia, encephalitis and death. An infected person spreads measles through coughs or sneezes. Once a person is infected, they are contagious from four days before their rash starts through four days afterwards. The period from exposure to the onset of symptoms is typically 10 to 14 days, but it can be longer. The Maine CDC said the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best prevention for measles. People who have been potentially exposed to measles should review their vaccine history and watch for symptoms, and those who are not immunized or do not know their measles immunization status should get vaccinated. The first confirmed Maine measles case of 2026, the state's first confirmed case since 2019, was announced by state health officials on Feb. 6. The Maine CDC then announced on Feb. 17 that four additional measles cases had been confirmed . More information is available on the Maine CDC's and U.S. CDC's webpages, as well as the Maine Immunization Program webpage . Photograph: George Frey/Getty Images Fourth person dies of measles-associated illness in US All deaths occurred in Pennsylvania, in worst year since 1992 for one of the most contagious diseases Pennsylvania health officials said a fourth person had died of measles-associated illness in the worst year for the disease since 1992. All four US deaths have occurred in the state. Due to the Trump administration changing how it reports measles deaths, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) does not count any of the deaths in its national tally. Three people died in 2025. “My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Dr Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s secretary of health, said in a statement. Pennsylvania has reported nearly 700 cases of measles. “We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the [measles, mumps and rubella] vaccine – which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades,” she said. One to three people per 1,000 die of measles-related complications, such as pneumonia and neurologic complications. The measles-associated death announced on Tuesday was of an 18-year-old Mifflin county resident, who was diagnosed with encephalomyelitis, a rare and severe neurological complication of the virus. Up to one in five people infected with the disease will be hospitalized. Pennsylvania’s agricultural areas in Lancaster and Mifflin counties have been the center of the state’s outbreak. Utah, Florida, Virginia and Texas have also seen dozens of cases, according to tracking from Johns Hopkins University. The US has seen more than 3,300 cases in 2026. Epidemiological data is generally considered an undercount. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, or MMR, prevents 97% of measles cases. However, vaccination rates among kindergarten-aged children, considered a bellwether, have experienced a slow decline as experts argue the administration spreads confusion among parents. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary and head of an anti-vaccine advocacy group before he took office, has upended federal vaccine policy and made multiple misleading statements about the MMR vaccine since taking office. The US eliminated measles in 2000, though it is unclear whether it can retain that status amid recent outbreaks. Globally, measles remains the leading cause of vaccine-preventable infant death. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Weather Local Investigations Videos U.S. & World Newsletters Partly Cloudy 72o Watch 24/7 Create profile / Log in Dashboard Email preferences Sign out Trending Watch 24/7 news Lindsay Clancy Patriots Decision 2026 Take our affordability survey Iran War Clear The Shelters Hub Today & Hub Happenings Expand 6 Weather Alerts Maine Maine CDC confirms measles case, warns of possible exposure at urgent care facility The Maine Centers for Disease Control has confirmed a measles case in a resident and is warning of possible exposure to anyone who visited a local urgent care facility last Saturday. By Marc Fortier • Published 6 hours ago • Updated 6 hours ago Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER Getty Creative Images Measles virus particle, illustration. This virus, from the Morbillivirus group of viruses, consists of an RNA (ribonucleic acid) core surrounded by an envelope studded with surface proteins haemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion protein, which are used to attach to and penetrate a host cell. Measles is a highly infectious itchy rash with a fever. It mainly affects children, but one attack usually gives life-long immunity. The Maine Centers for Disease Control has confirmed a measles case in a resident and is warning of possible exposure to anyone who visited a local urgent care facility last Saturday. The CDC says an unvaccinated adult from Somerset County tested positive for the illness, the first case in the state since February, when five cases were confirmed. Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE They said the latest case was confirmed on Tuesday, and anyone who was at the MaineGeneral Express Care, at 211 Main St. in Waterville, on Saturday, Sept. 12, between 8-11 a.m. might have been exposed to measles and should take precautions and watch for symptoms for 21 days after that date. The CDC said it is working with the facility to inform potentially exposed individuals. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, according to the CDC. If one person has measles, 90% of the people close to that person who are not immune will become infected. Symptoms include: Fever Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Rash that spreads from the head down. Those who develop symptoms are advised to contact their health care provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital to help prevent the spread of further infection. Login to the Member Center Make a donation Donate your car Corporate sponsorship CPR Shop Close Primary Navigation Politics Money Arts Justice Environment Newsletter Ways to support Some Coloradans may have been exposed to measles last week, earlier this week By John Daley · Sep. 16, 2026, 11:29 am Share: Julio Cortez/AP, File FILE - Vials of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are displayed Tuesday, Feb. 25, 2025. Updated at 3:42 p.m. on Friday, Sept. 18 Some Coloradans may have been exposed to measles at several locations throughout the state last week and this week. The warning comes after officials confirmed two cases of measles: one in an international visitor who traveled to Colorado last week, and another in an out-of-state traveler who visited earlier this week. Exposure locations include: Avanti Food and Beverage Boulder on Tuesday, Sept. 8 from 7 p.m. – 11:30 p.m. Gelto Boy on Boulder's Pearl Street Mall on Tuesday, Sept. 8 from 9:30 – 11:45 p.m. Denver Gem and Mineral Show in Westminster on Wednesday, Sept. 9 and Thursday, Sept. 10 Good Samaritan Hospital's emergency department in Lafayette on Friday, Sept. 11. from 7:30 – 8:30 p.m. Denver Union Station on Tuesday, Sept. 15 from 6 - 9 p.m. La Quinta Inn in Steamboat Springs on Wednesday, Sept. 15 from 9 a.m. - 2:30 p.m. Symptoms to watch for include fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed by a rash. If you were at the locations listed, watch for symptoms for 21 days after exposure. If you develop them, the best advice is to call your medical provider. The release said if you think you have measles symptoms and need medical care, don’t delay. The agency urges people to call their provider, urgent care or emergency department before going in to alert them you could have been exposed to measles — that simple step helps protect other people from possible exposure. It can stop further spread to others. 25 cases in Colorado this year So far in 2026, Colorado has recorded 25 measles cases — 22 of them were in unvaccinated people; one person had unknown vaccination status. Seven people have been hospitalized. This latest exposure comes after a relatively quiet summer on the measles front in Colorado. Since recording six cases in May, the health department reported no more than one case in each month since. Data Source: CDPHE Cases as of Sept. 16, 2026. Last year Colorado recorded 36 measles cases, the most by far in recent years. Before last year, the state recorded no more than one case each year since 2014, except in 2016 when it had two. Nationally, 2026 is the worst year for the disease since 1992. The CDC reports 3,294 people in the U.S. have caught measles in 2026, which compares with 2,289 last year. A fourth person in Pennsylvania died of illness-associated with measles, that state reported Tuesday. Last year, three people died from measles, according to the CDC. See Full Bio Follow: LocalNewskywnewsradio PHILADELPHIA (KYW Newsradio) — The Pennsylvania Department of Health has confirmed two more measles deaths on Tuesday, bringing the total for the state to four. Officials said the deaths were individuals in Jefferson and Mifflin counties. Both were unvaccinated. One was 18 years old, as confirmed by the Mifflin County Coroner’s office. The Jefferson County Coroner's office reported the death of a 40-year-old woman due to measles-associated illness. Late last month, the department confirmed the state's first two measles-related deaths in 35 years, both in Lancaster County. So far this year, there have been 693 confirmed cases in 38 counties. Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen said in a statement that her thoughts were with the families who lost loved ones to the highly contagious virus and that the state faces the worst measles outbreak in 30 years. “We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR vaccine — which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades,” Boden said. On social media, Gov. Josh Shapiro chastised the Trump administration, saying federal officials have stoked vaccine skepticism and misinformation, and accused Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy of compromising the work of public health agencies. “It is also deeply concerning to learn that [Kennedy] personally intervened in an otherwise administrative process to direct the CDC to not report these Pennsylvania deaths, presumably because it doesn’t fit his phony narrative,” he said. Health officials have urged people to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Over 99% of the state's cases this year have been in people who were unvaccinated.
